subsubtopic: TWENTY-FIFTH ANNIVERSARY OF RUSSIAN INVASION OF HUNGARY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this coming Friday marks the 25th anniversary of the invasion of Hungary by the U.S.S.R., a date that should be important to all those who cherish freedom. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour):
That this House condemn the U.S.S.R. for the events which began on October 23, 1956, and express its deep and abiding commitment to the return of a free democracy in Hungary and in all other nations similarly suppressed, and urge that the House leaders consider interrupting our proceedings on Friday, October 23, at noon so that we may observe one minute of silence in memory of those thousands who gave their lives in the fight for freedom and against totalitarianism.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. On behalf of the thousands of railway pensioners in Canada who have seen their pension income decimated by inflation, and who must have improved pensions if they are to have the quality of retirement which they deserve, and on behalf of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who, I am sure, would be moving such a motion were he able to be with us this afternoon, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Selkirk-Interlake (Mr. Sargeant):
That this House convey to the Canadian National Railways and to the Canadian Pacific Railway its wish that these two railway companies abandon their callous indifference about the well-being of former employees, immediately provide a significant cost of living increase to Canada's railway pensioners, and be willing to consider structured and regular protection of such pensioners as a way of avoiding for good the injustice which railway pensioners now suffer.

speechtext:

Whereas officials in the Department of Finance are recommending that the remission order on the taxation of northern benefits be discontinued, and whereas the ensuing unfairness and strife would likely result in large-scale strikes involving at least 10,000 Steelworkers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen):
That this House calls upon the Minister of National Revenue to keep his word to the electors of Labrador in his own constituency, as well as to other northern Canadians, and calls upon the Minister of Finance not to remove the remission order, thereby unfairly penalizing northern taxpayers.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in British Columbia we see evidence of growing concentration in the brewing industry. This past summer the three major brewing companies announced simultaneous price increases. Now Labatt's are planning to close their Victoria breweries, throwing 80 more people out of work. Therefore I move, seconded by the honourable and teetotalling member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett):

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION ON RECOMMENDATION RESPECTING RENT CONTROLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is to the minister responsible for housing who, I trust, has had an opportunity to read the CMHC report that was referred to yesterday by the Leader of the Opposition and by the Leader of the New Democratic Party. On page 4 the report reads in part:
It is important that provincial rent control bodies allow landlords to pass on the cost increases associated with mortgage renewals. The rent adjustments required to service the mortgage after renewal at current rent will exceed the maximum rent increases allowed under control regulations in certain provinces.
The recommendation is that landlords pass on these increases to tenants, which will result in extreme difficulty for a great many people. Has the minister accepted this recommendation put forward by CMHC? What plans does the minister have to provide some relief to what will be hard hit tenants?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION ON RECOMMENDATION RESPECTING RENT CONTROLS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in answer to the hon. member's question, I have not accepted the report. Indeed, the report has not been accepted by officials of Canada Mortgage and Housing. It was a document prepared by a person employed in the information section of the corporation.
In so far as the rental aspects are concerned, which the hon. member addresses, it was because of our concern for that market that this government reintroduced the capital cost allowance provisions discontinued by the government of which the hon. member was a part. We have reintroduced this in order to assist the supply side of the rental market so that people with low and moderate incomes can have alternate accommodation.

subsubtopic: MINISTER'S POSITION ON RECOMMENDATION RESPECTING RENT CONTROLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister has yet to tell us whether he has bothered to take the time to read the report which shows the housing industry in this country is in such a devastating crisis. I hope he will be able to assure us tomorrow that he has done so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, leaving the report aside, I want to come to another aspect of the housing industry. Even at the current level of housing starts, a level that would have been considered disastrous a couple of years ago, the residential housing industry is collapsing. The minister could have read that in the paper this morning. Supply companies, for example lumber companies, are also experiencing difficulty, which in turn is causing a tremendous loss of jobs, often in communities where a lumber
mill may be the major source of employment. There is a major spin-off effect when residential construction is in a slump. What does the minister plan to do?
Oh, oh!
What is your question?
I will be glad to put the question if the howling mob on the Liberal side of the House will just allow me some time to do it.
Hear, hear!
What is the minister going to do to prevent even further job losses in this very important sector of the economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the report to which the hon. member has referred was an interpretation of background information that I had requested from Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation earlier this summer. It was an interpretation of documentation that I have already seen. Therefore, in reading the report I was looking at another person's interpretation of the facts which, by and large, I think the member has indicated are generally known to the industry, to the public, and certainly to people in the House who interest themselves in the subject.
Do you?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Yes, I have looked at the report. In that sense it does not offer anything startlingly new except for misinterpretations.
As regards the strength of the industry itself, I would draw members' attention to a report in The Globe and Mail this morning which quotes one of the experts that is generally accepted as leading in so far as its reputation is concerned on analysis of the industry, Clayton Research. The figures of that company on starts are not as pessimistic as the figures the member would give us. For example, the article points out that in September starts were in the range of 190,000. It is the projection over the next 24 months with the assumption that interest rates will remain where they are that does pose problems. I would repeat that our concern for the industry and housing supply was the reason why this government supported the industry with the reintroduction of the capital cost allowance which was terminated by the previous government of which the hon. lady was a member.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the minister now says he has had a chance to read the CMHC report and that there is nothing new in it. I presume therefore that he verifies the figures contained in that report-
100,000	families going to lose their homes. The minister may not have the honesty to admit it, but the fact is that right now
October 20, 1981

there are many people in this country who cannot afford a home, or who have lost their homes and cannot find any place to rent because of the tight rental market.
My question concerns the situation in large metropolitan areas where the vacancy for rental apartments is nil, approaching zero. Hostels, which provide temporary relief, are overflowing. Mr. Minister, 22 people were reported sleeping in Toronto's city hall garage in this morning's paper, and these people cannot wait for a budget before trying to find better accommodation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member's questions are really extremely lengthy. The hon. member knows that questions should be brief.
Madam Speaker, my question is: what is the minister going to do about this pathetic situation in his own city, because in a country like this a situation of that nature is a disgrace?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, 1 believe 1 should take the opportunity, in answering the hon. member's question and in addressing her introduction, to say that I indicated I have read the report and I disagree with the report and the analysis that says that those people who pay over 30 per cent of their income toward shelter costs will lose their homes. I disagree with that, and I would like to take the opportunity of saying that to the hon. lady, lest she misinterpret me or not understand what I am saying to her.
With regard to people in the lower income levels and their need for shelter, I indicated to the leader of the NDP earlier this week that the federal government is not alone in its responsibility for serving people in their housing needs. The provinces, for example, administer the Emergency Housing Shelter Program, for example in metropolitan Toronto, and they, as well as municipalities, must assume some responsibility. I am happy to say that on Saturday of this weekend I attended a sod-turning ceremony, the start of construction of co-op housing in metropolitan Toronto under the auspices of the Metropolitan Toronto Labour Council which, by the way, says it appreciates Section 56(1) and is happy that the federal government is approaching and assisting people with moderate and low incomes.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE SOUGHT FOR HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. It is also related to housing. It is reported today that the federal housing minister, the Minister of Public Works, has made a firm promise that there will be assistance in the federal budget for home owners who are threatened by mortgage renewals. I would ask the Minister of Finance, first, if it is true that there will in fact be assistance provided in the budget for home owners? Second, will that assistance take into account the very high interest rates that a large number of Canadian families have been forced to assume over the course of the last four or five months, and therefore be retroactive in order to assist them in their plight as they try to hold on to their homes?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE SOUGHT FOR HOME OWNERS

Madam Speaker, all those points will be kept in mind. How I do it and with what measures, if any, is a matter the hon. member knows I cannot reveal before the budget. It is easy enough to ask whether "A" will be in the budget and whether "B" will be in the budget and, by a process of daily questioning, presumably, the budget would be

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if I may, I will put one final supplementary question to the minister responsible for housing. The minister is reported to have indicated that one flaw in the report we have been talking about for the last couple of days is that it concludes that anyone spending more than a set amount, 30 per cent of his income on shelter, is in danger of losing his home. The minister is quoted as having said:

speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration. As he knows, some 30,000 Polish refugees face a bleak winter in the camps in Austria. subsubtopic: MR. FULTON-ALLEGED OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE LEGAL OPINION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question of privilege arises from the speech given in the House yesterday by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) and also concerns the meeting of the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works on June
1.	At that committee meeting, while native people were present, I asked that a legal opinion be tabled regarding the implications of Bill C-48 in relation to the title of native people, particularly those north of 60, and as it relates to the whole of Canada lands as defined in the bill. At that time the minister said, and I quote, "Yes, I can give a legal opinion".
On August 31 the minister provided me with a letter in which he said this:
Further to my commitment to endeavour to obtain a legal opinion for the committee concerning the impact of Bill C-48 on land claims and aboriginal rights, I regret that I will be unable to meet your request-
Yesterday, following a speech given by the minister, with the unanimous agreement of the House I put a question to him asking for his views on the tabling of the legal opinion. It is crucial that every member of the House be aware of this opinion in order that we may vote in full knowledge of its implications for Bill C-48. At that time the minister had the following to say, and this is the fact upon which I base my prima facie case. I quote now from yesterday's Hansard at page 11922:
I meant that I would obtain a view in writing... The views I expressed then with respect to this ... are quite clearly founded on legal views I have obtained.
Madam Speaker, at the June meeting when native people were present, the minister promised to provide members of the committee with that legal opinion. In a letter to me he said that he was unable to provide it. Yesterday in this House during debate on Bill C-48, he said that he had received that legal opinion in writing, had looked at it but would not provide it to members of the House who have a crucial vote ahead of them.
I believe that a prima facie case of breach of privilege has been established. I agree with the ruling in Beauchesne that it is a question partly of law and partly of fact. Contempt of Parliament is a matter for this House to determine. This is the most serious contempt of this House that is possible. It strikes at the very root of the British common law, and the right of the aboriginal people to title to land.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. FULTON-ALLEGED OBLIGATION OF MINISTER TO TABLE LEGAL OPINION
speechtext:
Order, please. Of course the hon. member knows that ministers are not obligated to table legal opinions. They might seek them, and if I understand the argument, the minister said that what he was saying in the House flowed from the legal opinion that he had obtained. It is not a rule of the House that ministers are obligated to table legal opinions; it is a guideline which the government has set for itself. Any documents of this nature which eventually are tabled are always tabled because the government has decided that it feels
that the particular document may be tabled, but the minister is not obligated to table the document.
The question raised by the hon. member does not constitute the basis for a question of privilege. If the hon. member wants to take some action in order to force the minister to table the document, he may move a motion for the tabling of documents. That is the way in which he can proceed to get satisfaction.

Madam Speaker, I have been sitting on the edge of my chair day by day since last Thursday, waiting to hear from the government House leader. Indeed, I was rather hoping that we might have some House leaders' meetings so that we could have some idea of in what order the government intends to put the business of the House. As it is, after the expiration of today's business we are pretty well in the dark as to what will happen for the rest of the week.
We all have caucus tomorrow. It would be a relief, and perhaps even a resurrection of some faith in the ability of the government to manage, if the government House leader could inform us what is going to happen on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday and as far into next week as he can take us. I understand that this is a common practice, at least in Westminster. In that way we could have some time to plan ahead and inject some order into the business of the House, thereby assisting the government to achieve a level of efficiency which, I am sure, they would be glad to achieve with our assistance.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Madam Speaker, actually, I could refer my hon. colleague to the reply I gave last Thursday, but out of politeness I shall repeat what I told him last week, which is public knowledge. We are considering Bill C-48, and until we have some indication as to when debate at the report and third reading stages of this very important bill, which contains a number of amendments as my hon. colleague is aware, will be completed it is useless for me to speculate on what the business of the House will be during the next few days. However, if the member for Yukon should tell me that we are about to dispose of Bill C-48, 1 shall immediately call a meeting and examine the Order Paper with him in order to determine what measures can be considered within the very short term. The answer I gave last Thursday, which I have just repeated at this point, is that with the exception of today, which is an opposition day, Bill C-48 is on the agenda and we shall be dealing with this bill tomorrow and Thursday. However, as I told the hon. member last week, we shall probably be holding a meeting of the House leaders on Thursday, when we usually meet to plan the business for the following week. I suggest that the hon. member follow established practice and wait until Thursday when we can discuss the business of the following week. In addition-I am sorry I did not hear what the former Solicitor General for nine months was saying.
Nobody pays any attention to convention.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The hon. member says that no one pays any attention to convention. That is right. When I read the opposition motion today, it stated:
Business of the House
-notwithstanding any Standing Order, practice or precedent, the House does not regard the passage of this motion as a vote of non-confidence in the government.

To answer the question put by my colleague for Yukon, first of all I wish to thank him for his offer of co-operation, and I can assure him that I will take his offer very seriously. I was planning to hold a meeting Thursday, but if he should tell me that we will dispose of Bill C-48 tomorrow, I am quite willing to hold this meeting before Thursday. However, if he cannot give me that assurance, I see no urgent reason for having a meeting before Thursday. Right after Question Period on Thursday afternoon, I shall be happy to answer the usual question on House business or to rise on a point of order to provide further information on House business for the following week.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I thank the government House leader for that confirmation as to the business for the remainder of this week. I might say, in response to his reply to the intervention by my friend, the hon. member for Durham-Northumberland, that that last paragraph was placed in the motion precisely to assist the hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Northumberland-Miramichi, and other hon. members who might like to vote for the very reasonable opposition motion which has been put today, the subject matter for debate today.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would like to reassure the House leader of the Progressive Conservative Party and tell him that my colleagues on this side of the House understand the rules quite well, and that despite the indications of the opposition party, they are bound by our Standing Orders; and while some of them might favour more railway lines in Canada, they do not necessarily also favour elections at this time.
Those of my colleagues to whom the hon. member has just referred are quite aware that we are dealing with a harmless parliamentary tactical plan, but I believe that these are important matters which would have required a more serious approach. I remember that last June or July, when my hon. friend was not House leader for his party, the Progressive Conservative Party tried to make a mockery of the debate on capital punishment by binding the opinions of the hon. members to a non-confidence vote. The same little parliamentary tactical plan is now being used, and in my opinion, it is unfortunate to try to degrade a serious debate by forcing the hon. members to support a motion and take a stand on whether or not they want elections to be held at this time.
All this is therefore very clear. Government members are not fooled by such tactics. We understand the parliamentary procedure for the business of supply, and Standing Order 58(9), which deals very clearly with the motion of the Progressive Conservative Party, states that this rule applies and that

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Today the House is confronted with a motion under the terms of Standing Order 58(9), which calls for a vote this evening and which, according to the Standing Order, therefore amounts to a vote of non-confidence in the government. The last paragraph of that motion, however, suggests that the passage of this motion should not be considered as a vote of non-confidence in the government.
There is nothing in the Standing Orders to guide the Speaker in the interpretation of what constitutes a vote of non-confidence. In the past my predecessors have made certain comments on this problem, but have chosen not to interfere with the right of an hon. member of the opposition to move a motion under Standing Order 58(9).
The motion will be moved, debated and voted upon as provided for in the Standing Orders.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE

speakeroldname: Hon. Yvon Pinard (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to be able to rely on the opinion of my learned colleague, but I must unfortunately point out with all due respect that I cannot do so because he had the choice of moving his business of supply motion under two paragraphs of Standing Order 58, that is either paragraph (9) or paragraph (11). If he reads both paragraphs closely, he will realize that if he wants a vote by roll call, despite what he would like to do, he must proceed under paragraph (9) of Standing Order 58, which calls for a non-confidence vote.
In other words, what he is trying to do is to amend unilaterally the Standing Orders of the House because what he is asking us amounts to saying: Let us have a vote under paragraph (9) of Standing Order 58, but let us not disregard paragraph (9) under consideration because we do not want it to be a non-confidence vote. To do what he asks, we would need the unanimous consent of the House and we would have to follow the usual procedure to amend the implementation of our Standing Orders. However, this has not been done and I do not believe that he intends to do so. In this case, he has chosen paragraph (9) of Standing Order 58 which calls for a vote of non-confidence, and we are bound by the Standing Orders. We have no choice. He should have simply requested an allotted day under paragraph (11) of Standing Order 58. He would then have had no problem. He would have had his debate and the House would not have had to vote on a non-confidence motion against the government.
In conclusion, what I want to say is this: it is not up to the Leader of the Opposition to determine the value of paragraph (9) of Standing Order 58. The rules are there and we are bound by the Standing Orders, which tell us that when a motion calls for a vote under Standing Order 58(9), it is automatically a vote of non-confidence, and this is confirmed by the terms used in paragraph (11) of the same Standing Order 58. Obviously, in view also of the notice printed in the Order Paper, we have no choice but to vote against this motion if we want to avoid a vote of non-confidence against the government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE

I simply want to point out to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition that this is precisely what I stated in the last paragraph, namely that this motion will be moved, debated and voted on as provided in our Standing Orders. That is all. This motion will be decided by the House. However, it was my duty to point out to members of this House that the motion before them had been moved under the provisions of Standing Order 58(9) and that one of the paragraphs of this motion seemed contradictory to the provisions of Standing Order 58(9). It was my duty to point this out to the House. However, as I have said, I shall not become involved in the debate on the interpretation of what constitutes a non-con-

fidence motion against the government. I believe that the House can settle this issue in the usual way.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
That this House expresses its deep concern over the abandonment of 19 per cent of the VIA Rail passenger network, which will take place when Order in Council P.C. 1981-2171 is implemented on November 15, 1981;
that the House recommends that the government delay the implementation date for Order in Council P.C. 1981-2171 to at least September 27, 1982, the date commuter rail service in Quebec and Ontario is presently scheduled to terminate under the same order;
that this House refers the subject-matter of Order in Council P.C. 1981-2171 to the Standing Committee on Transport to enable the committee to evaluate the economic, social, statistical and legal basis for the decision to diminish rail service, and instructs the committee to report its conclusions and recommendations to the House by June 30, 1982; and
that, to facilitate the support of this motion by all honourable members, and notwithstanding any Standing Order, practice or precedent, the House does not regard the passage of this motion as a vote of non-confidence in the government.
He said: Madam Speaker, at the outset I must say it is quite obvious that hon. members on the other side are scrambling and a bit nervous over this motion. But contrary to what the government House leader has said, the motion is not put forth in the context of being a tactic. It is a very reasonable motion. It is a responsible and realistic motion. It is not meant or intended to offend or embarrass anyone. I want to say very clearly and unequivocally that the motion is put forward in a sincere and constructive manner.
I believe, notwithstanding what the government House leader has said, that it does deserve the consideration and support of all hon. members who support the principle of fairness. The motion also deserves the consideration and support of all of those who believe that we need an adequate rail passenger system in this country. It is also important for members on all sides of the House to recognize that rail passenger service, rather than being considered a mode of the past, is indeed a mode of the future. This motion gives all hon. members an opportunity to recognize that with higher energy prices now is not the time to be cutting back rail passenger services or public forms of transportation. We should be engaged in efforts to expand these kinds of services rather than reducing them.
Lastly, this motion gives all hon. members an opportunity to associate themselves with the very severe hardships that will be imposed upon hundreds of thousands of Canadians who will be deprived of service when that service is withdrawn, and who will have no other alternative. There will be hundreds, if not thousands of people who will be losing their jobs. This will have an impact upon their families. There will be uprooting of

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
families. People will have to move to other localities. There will be many others who will be affected indirectly as well as a result of these cuts. There may be others who will be facing very serious decisions and urgent consequences. In particular I am thinking of the small-business men who rely very heavily upon rail passenger service, especially in areas where tourism is an important fact of life. In short, we believe that the impact of these cuts will deliver irreparable social and economic damage to various regions throughout the country.
Furthermore, we have reason to believe that there are a number of members on the other side of the House who are not in support of this decision. This motion clearly gives them an opportunity to stand and vote and to make their position known.
We believe that the cutback decision should be deferred. It should be deferred on the basis that there are a number of factors that were not taken into consideration when this decision was made. As we recall, this decision to cut back services was taken by the minister and his cabinet colleagues in a unilateral, arbitrary manner. We believe that decision is shortsighted, illogical and very damaging. The decision was announced when the House was not in session. Instead the minister made this major policy announcement by way of a press conference and press release. The decision was conveniently deferred until the House of Commons had adjourned, and I might add the House was forced to adjourn as a result of closure.
There are a number of reasons why we take exception to both the decision and the process. First, we believe that the minister and his colleagues have not accurately assessed the very severe social and economic damages that this decision will inflict upon countless hundreds of thousands of Canadians.
We contend, and this has been proved beyond a shadow of a doubt, that the massive bulk of the train services that are being discontinued are used very heavily. They are needed. There is also no alternative means of transportation offered to those people who will be forced to survive without rail passenger service.
Let me look at the Toronto to Barrie run. I quoted these figures the other day and I think they are worthy of quoting again. For example, the Toronto to Barrie run has seven to eight coaches carrying 425 to 500 passengers in each direction daily. The Toronto to Stouffville run carries 300 to 350 passengers in each direction daily. The Toronto to Havelock run carries 200 to 275 passengers in each direction daily. The Winnipeg to Jasper and Vancouver Supercontinental carries an average of 350 passengers, and that figure obviously goes down in the winter and goes up in the summer. The Montreal to Mont-Laurier weekend service carries 1,200 to 1,600 people. That is the number of people who use this single service.
Let us go to the Atlantic service which has been described as the most successful train service of the whole VIA Rail system. That was stated by a senior official of VIA Rail. In the winter
months this train averages between 200 and 250 passengers, and in the summer months the Atlantic averages between 400 to 600 passengers. It is very clear that these services are used and are needed.
It is also important to recognize that during the 1977-78 period there were some very extensive hearings conducted by the Canadian Transport Commission during which they reviewed the needs of Canadians relative to rail passenger services. They brought forth a structure which they described as an irreducible minimum. What this decision is doing is essentially flying in the face of that decision which was arrived at through consultation and extensive public hearings.
I would also deal with the other impact, which is the direct loss of jobs. The minister has indicated that 1,600 jobs will be directly affected. However, there will be countless hundreds of other jobs that will be dislocated as a result of these cutbacks. We have already had an announcement by CN that 560 positions in CN's three main shops will be affected with one fifth of the positions being affected in Moncton, two fifths in Montreal and two fifths in Winnipeg.
We also have further evidence. The Winnipeg Labour Council estimates the job loss in the greater area of Winnipeg will be no less than 500. VIA Rail has also issued some 313 lay-off notices, 166 occurring in western Canada and 133 in the Atlantic region and the province of Quebec.
The impact on small business, particularly the tourist industry, is another aspect of concern. We have one community which will be hit extremely hard, the community of Jasper. It is basically a one-industry town, its major industry being tourism. There has been well documented evidence that between $6 million and $10 million worth of tourist revenue will be lost as a result of the withdrawal of this service. We all know as well, and I put this on the record yesterday, that some 25,000 Japanese tourists who come to this country use the train when visiting us and they are big spenders, spending an average of $2,000 per person in addition to their transportation and accommodation. That tourist potential is threatened by these cutbacks.
I could go on and on but my other colleagues will be elaborating further on the specific impacts that will result in the various regions of Canada.
The second reason we have serious doubts about this decision is based on the matter of the rationale used by the minister in bringing this decision forward. First of all I have to say it is really very difficult to understand how the minister can revitalize the system by abandoning it. I really do not understand that and I hope he will attempt to enlighten us. We know that this is largely a political decision.
On the question of data, the data have been challenged in every corner of the country. There is inaccurate information. Costs are inflated and revenues are understated. There are a lot of questions arising from the fact that many of these statistics are outdated. In many cases we have estimates of load factors and occupancy rates that are outdated. In a very global way there is a shortage of data and, furthermore, there
October 20, 1981

are serious questions and suspicions about the accuracy and relevancy of that data. As a result, this creates a large gap in terms of public confidence when the minister and his officials try to rationalize the reasons behind these cutbacks.
The minister says there is to be a saving of $100 million as a result of these cutbacks. Some $30 million of that will have to be paid toward labour people giving them assistance in job retraining and job relocation, so we really get down to $70 million. One really has to question whether, by reducing the services and taking away that revenue potential which is generated as a result without appreciably reducing those fixed costs, that savings of $100 million can really be realized.
The third reason we have serious reservations about this decision is that we do not believe VIA Rail has been given a fair chance. Quite frankly it is hardly a legitimate offspring. The problem of VIA Rail can probably be described best by one word, and that is "neglect". As a matter of fact, if we look at the 1980 report we will see that 1980 was the first year in which VIA Rail had control over all rail passenger services in this country. That really becomes a benchmark for its future. It is really strange that while it has had one full year of operation in control of all rail passenger services in 1981, it is going to be emasculated to the point that one fifth of the rail passenger service in this country will be lost. Notwithstanding the fact that it has had the cards stacked against it, it has increased its ridership by 41 per cent since 1976 or 1977. The occupancy rate is well over 50 per cent. It has not been given sufficient resources. The equipment being used is archaically out of date. As a matter of fact, when we look at the statistics of the equipment inventory we find that 67 per cent of the equipment used by VIA Rail is between 26 and 30 years of age; 23 per cent of its equipment is over 30 years of age. As a matter of fact, VIA is still using, I believe, 102 units which are air-conditioned through ice-activated mechanisms, so they are hopelessly out of date in terms of upgrading the equipment to realistic modern technology.
It is true that VIA has not been given sufficient rersources to re-equip. It is true that VIA has not had the necessary autonomy or a clearly defined mandate described by government and/or Parliament. It has not had a realistic costing order, which accounts for about 63 per cent of its total expenditures. It has not had proper contractual arrangements in its dealings with the railroads. It still has done reasonably well notwithstanding the fact that it has old equipment and paid some $70 million to both railways for equipment that would probably have been scrapped had VIA not been created.
There are some very major questions regarding those aspects, but the biggest question revolves around the costing order. The costing order really strikes at the heart and the core of the issues we are debating. The operating agreement signed between VIA and the railways locked VIA into a payment system which has contributed greatly to its present state of crisis. It is hard to believe, but charges have escalated beyond control. In his testimony before the Commons committee the president made this point very emphatically. He said that charges for transportation and maintenance represent well
VIA Rail
over 60 per cent of VIA's entire expense budget. The CTC costing order serves as a basis for these charges and it was agreed to by all parties including VIA, the railways and the government. I am told the corresponding level of costs for Amtrak, its neighbour to the south, is something in the order of 25 per cent.
This order was developed in 1969 as a means of prorating railway costs to passenger services performed and were then the basis of subsidy payments to the railways in compensation for these losses under the National Transportation Act of 1968. In those days the railways dealt only with the Canadian Transport Commission which audited and verified the costs claimed under the costing order and authorized corresponding subsidy payments.
The railways had originally helped to establish the basic rules of allocation under R-6313. They naturally had a vested interest in seeing that the allowances were generous, and also that the rules were changed and interpreted to make them even more generous. Costing order R-6313 has now apparently evolved into a system designed to allocate long-term variable rather than short-term avoidable costs to the passenger services and the difference is profound. The new levels may be as much as twice as high as the former levels. Moreover, the costing order works as a sort of honour system whereby the railways make the allocations and the government, or VIA, pays.
Post auditing by the CTC runs behind and is limited to a review of methodology and bases of charges and not to the actual levels of services. That is where you have this matter of the thirteenth billing that Mr. Roberts keeps complaining about. I might say that in 1980 I believe the payments to both railways amounted to somewhere in the order of $356 million. That is essentially the core of the problem.
It is interesting to note that what we are really dealing with here is that the railways are submitting bills to VIA Rail which VIA Rail has no way of challenging, bills which are basically openended, which are cost-plus. It is similar to what the railways in the United States wanted when Amtrak was set up. They chose a different route.
I am quoting now from a report to the Congress of the United States by the U.S. comptroller general. He referred to VIA and said:
The railroads charged Amtrak $305 million in fiscal year 1980, accounting for
over one fourth of Amtrak's operating expenses-
It goes on to point out that in negotiating the original agreements, the railways wanted Amtrak reimbursed for all their direct costs, the passenger services and facilities, plus an array of other payments for indirect costs, management fees, return on investment and profit. Since Amtrak was taking over substantial passenger losses from the railroads, it believed Congress intended for it to pay no more than the direct operating costs of the trains the railroads would be running and not pay the railroads a profit. Accordingly, Amtrak negotiated contracts requiring payment only for railroad

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
expenses incurred solely for the benefit of passenger services, plus payments for certain costs common to freight and passenger service determined to be avoidable for the railroads if passenger services had not been provided. That is a very fundamental difference.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: It is the same thing.

speechtext:
The minister says it is the same thing. I hope he can prove that to us today in the course of the debate. It is a fundamental difference.
In the case of VIA, the charges are not fair. The minister must be in total and fundamental disagreement with the chairman and president of VIA Rail because that gentleman says the situation is unfair. VIA Rail wants to go to fixed base contracts. Why has the minister not done something about this? Why has the minister not rescinded R-6313 rather than-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Why didn't you?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: We were considering it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: That is for sure.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: You were studying it. I am studying it too.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: The charges are not fair. The minister knows that. It is really a bookkeeping item. Rather than a major dismantling as the minister is proposing, a new costing order should be arranged. The minister knows that. He could use Section 64 to rescind costing order R-6313. He could do that very easily. He is so anxious to use R-6313 to take away passenger services from Canadians. Why does he not do something to get his own house in order?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: I will.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
We seriously question the legal and moral right of the minister arbitrarily to slash rail services in this country by 20 per cent without following the traditional practice. We believe the minister's actions constitute a violation of the spirit of the National Transportation Act and, indeed, the intent of Section 64. Quite frankly, we believe that it denies Canadians the opportunity to apply the rules of natural justice. I could go on for some time on this theme.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is dangerous. It establishes a dangerous precedent. It undermines the integrity of the CTC. Will the CTC be abolished with the same stroke of the pen that the minister has used to abolish one fifth of VIA Rail services in this country? He may as well because it was so crassly circumvented, Mr. Speaker. As a minimum he should now take steps to ensure that the role of the CTC is clarified.
What does all this mean? If the minister is allowed to get away with this, does it mean he can now unilaterally and arbitrarily abandon any branch line in western Canada as he sees fit? The basic network is guaranteed to the year 2000.
The minister, if he is allowed to get away with this, with one stroke of the pen could dismantle the basic network.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Hypothetically, yes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: The minister agrees with me. That is very dangerous.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Hypothetically.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
What about ferry services? The federal government provides some $200 million in support of ferry services. If he decides unilaterally and arbitrarily to discontinue that support, could he do it? I suspect he could. If he gets away with this, I suspect he could do that.
What about the statutory freight rates? They are enshrined in the same law as Sections 260, 261, 262 which guarantee some semblance of rail passenger services in this country. If the minister is allowed to get away with this with just a stroke of the pen, he could undo the statutory freight rates.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: That's right. And he would.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
We know that CN and CP have never been relieved of their responsibility to provide rail passenger services. That was never done when VIA Rail was established. What does that mean? If VIA withdraws, are CN and CP responsible for providing those passenger services? These things must be clarified.
Consider air services. The minister could unilaterally dismantle air services to any community in Canada if he is allowed to get away with this. He says it is in the public interest. He says he knows what is best. He does away with 20 per cent of VIA services this year. He could repeat that again next year and he probably will. The minister should not get away with this, Mr. Speaker. The implications are too far-reaching. He thinks he is on the right course and he is proceeding with a great deal of assurance and confidence. Yet he chooses to ignore the traditional process which is part of the Canadian way, the right to hold public hearings, to be heard and have an opportunity to express concern about the criteria of public convenience and necessity. This has all really gone down the drain. If the minister is so sure he is right, why does he refuse to take his case to the people, to the court of the CTC, or the court of the transportation committee?
Another thing which is very disturbing, Mr. Speaker, is that there was not one word mentioned about the dismantling of rail passenger service by the Liberal party in the last election. Not one word. There was not a word mentioned about the changes to the constitution, for that matter. Nor did we hear anything about the doubling of energy prices. So I suppose in that regard they were at least consistent.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: They talked about double track.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Yes, we did hear a lot about double tracking. We can only conclude that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dropped his double track and all we have in its place, rather than "double-track Trudeau", is "no-train Pepin".
October 20, 1981

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: We got double-crossed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
The fifth point, and perhaps the most important, is that there are alternatives to the cuts the Minister of Transport is proposing. I have mentioned that there are changes which can be made to the costing order. There should be improvements in the contractual arrangements between the railways and VIA Rail. We should give VIA Rail the necessary autonomy, power and clout to negotiate with the railways in a business like manner. The VIA Rail mandate should be clarified and enshrined in legislative form. Surely there are improvements which can be made in terms of productivity and the trimming of frills and supervisory and administrative fat. I think there is a clear indication that those who are using rail passenger services are prepared to pay a little more for them provided they are retained and improved. I think it is fair to say that schedules can be improved. Market improvements are certainly something which can be looked at. We have seen some very new approaches to tourist development.
The CTC has made a number of proposals, but there are four specific alternatives which have come up since the announcement of the minister to disband 20 per cent of the rail passenger service. One of them is contained in a leaked document which ended up in the hands of the Toronto Star, which points out that there is a proposal in which the Atlantic and the Supercontinental could be salvaged. The alternate proposal is estimated to be $2.4 million per year cheaper to operate than the government's proposal, based upon existing operations and costing methods. That clearly is one proposal which should be considered.
The second proposal is one which has been advanced by Transport 2000 which sets out to re-equip the Transcontinentals. Transport 2000 points out that an investment in new bilevel equipment would decrease operating costs by 31 per cent and that a combination of increased passenger revenues and the reduction of operating costs would reduce losses by some 52 per cent. Transport 2000 goes on further to point out that that capital which is invested in the re-equipment of the rolling stock could be paid for in seven and half years.
A third alternative was advanced by the government of Alberta. It is a very constructive, positive and responsible approach. It too involves the re-equipping of the western Transcontinental. It points out that costs could be reduced by somewhere between one half and two thirds of existing expenditures. The equipment and infrastructure would cost some $100 million. The total capital cost could be recovered through operating economies within a two year period. It also made another recommendation relative to payments to the railways based upon avoidable costs rather than the full associated costs with penalties and with bonuses included.
Then we have a fourth alternative proposal which comes from VIA Rail itself. It is very strange that after the study by Transport 2000 and the study by the government of Alberta were released we have a study appearing from VIA Rail itself wherein it too proposes the re-equipping of one train from
VIA Rail
Halifax to Vancouver for a cost of $200 million, and I understand it would cost $100 million to re-equip the other one. Was this information given to the minister before his decision was made? Does he know? Is he aware? Why was it not given to the Standing Committee on Transport? Why was it not given to members of the House of Commons so that this matter could be looked into and we would have all the facts? What is the minister hiding? What is he afraid of? Why is he hiding these things?
There are clear alternatives to the decision which has been made by the Minister of Transport. Is it asking too much to have the legislators of this country examine those alternatives or the people of this country look at those alternatives? Surely not.
This is a serious issue. It is a national issue. It is an issue which strikes at the very fundamental core of Canadian confederation, and I want to say in conclusion that I believe the government has grossly underestimated the deep feeling which exists in the hearts and minds of Canadians about the fact that rail passenger service is a link which binds this country together and keeps it united. To many it is more important than the Constitution. It is a fundamental part of confederation. We would not have been a country had it not been for the guarantees inherent in the provision of rail services.
For this reason and for the other reasons I have cited, I commend this motion to all hon. members. I hope it will be given their earnest attention and that they will see fit to support it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not at all underestimated the public reaction to my announcement of July 27. As a matter of fact, I did not expect any applause and telegrams of congratulations but the government and I thought at the time and continue to think that this is the best thing we could do under the circumstances.
But people do not like it when services to which they are accustomed are suddenly being reduced, even when, collectively, they are using them less and less, and when, individually, they are not using them at all. There are some 24 million people in Canada; well, last year, VIA Rail sold 7 million tickets to the travelling public. When we realize that these include the tickets bought by commuters who travelled by train much more than once that year, we can assume that there are probably 20, 21, or maybe 22 million Canadians who never saw the inside of a train compartment that year. And yet, when we raise the possibility of cutting down on the number of rail routes, everybody or nearly everybody feels compelled to object. There are even some people who wrote to me to inquire whether I was really aware that I was attacking an extremely important Canadian symbol, a symbol which I indeed respect and which has enormously contributed to the development of our country, adding that I was thus attacking

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
the monarchy, which I find somewhat strange personally. I suggest that it is the current nostalgia for the rail era which is going against the government's decision.

There is one word in the motion which obviously is of paramount importance, and that word is "delay". The purpose of the motion is to delay. That is quite normal. When confronted with change-change that they have called for repeatedly-most people hesitate and procrastinate. I also do it occasionally! I am sure others are in the same position.
However, I was surprised that the hon. member for Vegre-ville (Mr. Mazankowski) should attach his name to this motion. I have great respect for him, as he knows. I think we can call ourselves friends. I listened to what he said, very carefully, not too long ago, on June 11, 1980. Speaking to the Transportation Research Forum in what was meant to be a program speech about what, unfortunately for him, he was not able to do because of his too short term in office as minister of transport, he said a number of things, and I will quote a couple of them. He said, for example, at page 9 of his speech:
Steps will have to be taken to reduce unnecessary operation costs.. . Current high levels of service will not be able to be maintained indefinitely-
On the passenger side of rail transportation, the ever increasing debt incurred by the federal government in subsidies is a major problem which will have to be dealt with.

Steps will have to be taken to increase the efficiency and utilization of current facilities, reduce unnecessary operation costs and, generally, to make better use of what now exists.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE

On the passenger side of rail transportation, the ever increasing debt incurred by the federal government in subsidies is a major problem which will have to be dealt with. This fiscal year alone, $424 million-
He knows now it is $450 million.
-will go toward subsidizing rail passenger service. This is especially urgent when considering the impact on rail's competition, the bus mode. If the principle of equal treatment among modes is applied-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. If the minister is going to be quoting speeches of other members of the House, would he mind quoting the speeches as they are written and not edit them so that they make a case exactly contrary to that actually being made?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when there is an obvious typing error in a text one is entitled to say "sic" after the word. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, there was absolutely nothing revolutionary in the decision we took on July 27 since it was basically aimed at stabilizing VIA Rail's operational budget to the benefit of its capital budget. It had been recommended in a number of previous studies and reports. Mr. Lang had reached that decision in 1976, or nearly so, but he was not in a position to implement it for the reasons we all know.
I would even suggest that had the hon. member for Vegre-ville had more time he would have done so himself. Short of drastically increasing his budget, the president of VIA Rail fully agrees, and I quote the statement he made recently:
I think we now have a solid foundation from which we can go ahead-
Those are the words of the president, Mr. Roberts. And if the decision had not been taken it would have become inevitable to act, if you want, in a piecemeal fashion, haphazardly and especially without the dramatic and rapid increases in the VIA Rail capital budget which will enable the company to put more LRCs in service. I am referring to the light, rapid and comfortable units produced by Bombardier which will be rolling in western Canada and in the maritimes in the next two or three years.
I said recently-

October 20, 1981

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: When?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: In the next two or three years-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: When?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
In the next two or three years. I do not think you would have had them, had the July decision not been made. [Translation]
Mr. Speaker, I said recently that a number of people who are blasting me today and who are blasting the government for doing what we did will praise us in two or three years, while riding in their light, rapid and comfortable trains.

In this debate I have to prove, and I will do so repeatedly- and I might say I am willing to go to the transportation committee if that is the wish of hon. members-that the decision is a responsible one from a budgetary point of view and from a transportation point of view. It is also consistent with trends in Canada and elsewhere in the world. If my friends want to look they will see that what I have recommended here is being done in any country they can name. I will show them that the same general policy is being followed.
I am not being original. I am being banal. I am not being eccentric. The matter of non-recourse to the Canadian Transport Commission for public hearings is not only legal, but is wise and justified. It is the only way to go. I will try to demonstrate that more extensively in a moment.
Also, the decision is consistent with our energy-saving preoccupations and policies. There is nothing more spendthrift than a locomotive pulling 15 cars that are three quarters empty, as is so often the case.
The decision respects the interests of railway workers by allocating $30 million to assist them in adjusting to this decision. The amount of money is extraordinarily high. I want to say also that it is not unfriendly to VIA. I have already indicated that the VIA leadership is in agreement with it.
[ Translation]
I said that our decision was consistent, necessary and responsible as far as the budget is concerned. No doubt I will be accused of being obsessed by profits and losses, it is entirely untrue. I know quite well that VIA will never pay for its own way, there has never been such a railway in the world. My criterion is not at all profits, it is not even breaking even, but there are, Mr. Chairman, some limits to what the government can earmark for unpopular services, especially in the present period of budgetary restraint.
Mr. Chairman, you are well aware of the figures which I will quickly quote. The government contribution to VIA in
1980-	81 was $450 million and it will reach $490 million in
1981-	82. Well, from that amount, $332 million were set aside for the operational deficit which on an average regularly
VIA Rail
increases by 20 per cent per year while $117 million were allotted to investment deficit financing this year.
As you can see, Mr. Speaker, that is almost, in fact it is more than, twice the amount allotted VIA by the government in 1977-78, namely $209 million. Subsidies therefore went from $209 to $450 million; they now amount to $490 and will soon reach $565 million. So, we see the rate is on the increase. That is not without importance. It may be worth it to point out in passing that government assistance to VIA, and the people of Canada indirectly, represents one quarter of the total Department of Transport budget. So, one fourth of the $2 billion of the Ministry of Transport will in fact be used to move passengers by train.
I have already mentioned that last year VIA Rail had seven million passengers. So, if you divide the $490 million in subsidies paid VIA Rail in that year by seven million passengers, you see that every time a person buys a ticket, the Ministry of Transports pays out $70. In the case of the Transcontinental, the figure amounts to about $160. Taking specific figures, for instance the trip from Vancouver to Montreal, the ticket will cost $191 and the Government of Canada will add another $443. If you go from Montreal to Chicoutimi, it will cost you $21 and the government $180.
I could give you all the figures, which would not fail to impress certain persons. As for the capacity rate, the average is 46 per cent for the whole network, but many lines average 5, 10, 15 per cent and no more than that. The same applies to the cost-revenue ratio: the average amounts to 30 per cent, which means that VIA recovers, on an average, only 30 per cent of its costs. But in fact there are lines where the cost-revenue ratio is only 2, 3, 10 or 15 per cent. I say this-I beg your pardon?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Those are your figures!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Obviously we have not counted all the individuals who passed through the doors. That is a very hard thing to do, one would have to increase twofold the number of VIA employees to arrive at a precise figure. Nevertheless, and I am speaking here to the Leader of the Opposition, if we look at this data generally, what we are presenting here is an undeniable fact. In any event, it is not only in Canada, that the number of rail passengers has dropped, this has occurred all over the world, in Japan, in Great Britain, even in France. We are not making this up. The situation which exists in Canada today can also be found in the United States and in other large countries. Therefore, although the figures may not be accurate to the very last digit, there is obviously a definite trend here, even if it cannot be proven with figures that are accurate to the last decimal. It is interesting to see people's reaction when you give them these figures. I have done that several times recently. For example, Geoff Johnson of the Ottawa Citizen wrote a very interesting article in May 1980, and I quote:

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
For every passenger that travels by train the Canadian taxpayer loses 19.4 cents per mile. Theoretically, he says the government could send every rail passenger by air, pick up the entire tab and still save millions of dollars.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: That is false.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
No, that is true. This is the same newspaperman who some weeks ago said that I was the worst thing to happen to the railways since Jesse James. Obviously, he is a bit ambivalent but never misses the chance of making a good joke and that was a good one.
Similarly, you can read some reactions of members of the press. A columnist for the Edmonton Journal-I am sure the Leader of the Opposition would appreciate my source-was on the same track when he said:
We cannot say on the one hand that the government spends too much and on the other call for retention of a service used by so few.
There are a great many people in Canada who believe there should be limitations. The government does not have the responsibility to maintain trains if a sufficient number of people do not wish to use them.
The Vancouver Province on August 5, 1981 said this:
In general, the reduction in service is to be applauded because it has checked mounting losses and given VIA some hope of being able to improve those services it retains. This is sensible.
I have quoted from the west particularly because I expected some of my hon. friends from the west to be present in the House today.

So what are we to do under the circumstances? In 1976, Mr. Lang proposed a substantial cutback in subsidies. The decision announced on July 27 does not even include that. In fact, we will be increasing the total subsidies, as I indicated, from $450 million to $490 million in 1981-82, to $506 million in 1982-83 and to $537 million in 1983-84, at least to account for inflation. So there is no cutback in government aid to VIA, far from it, we will be increasing it. What we are doing is setting a ceiling, a maximum on the operating deficit, we are saying that it will remain at $365 million for 1981-82, $367 million in
1982-83 and $355 million in 1983-84. So that is what we are doing, we are putting a freeze on VIA's level of operating costs. We are converting this money to capital expenditures for VIA Rail, and those capital expenditures will go from $90 million to $117 million, to $125 million in 1981-82, to $129 million in 1982-83, and to $182 million in 1983-84. You can readily see how very fast the capital budget of VIA Rail is growing. It amounts to $446 million in three years. Why exactly are we doing this? It is because the problem comes in fact from the vicious circle in which VIA Rail is now operating in having to attract customers and provide good service, which increases its operating costs, and of not having the capital required to make the needed basic investments.
That is the reasoning, and what we are doing now is extraordinarily simple. We are saying to VIA Rail: Listen, you have outmoded equipment which is 25 or 30 years old. Renew your stock right away and provide good service to the population, and if you do so, the number of users will increase. To do so, operating costs and deficits must be kept down to $350 or $365 million, and to do so, there ...ust be cutbacks. That is the only way to do it.
The other option, which the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) seemed to support, would have been to negotiate an additional amount of $100 million or $200 million to VIA Rail and to prolong the current agony of VIA Rail, because this money would have gone for operating costs rather than capital expenditures. This is a very simple reasoning which is certainly not original, as I have said repeatedly. [English]
The decision also is responsible from the point of view of transportation policy. It helps to define the role of railway passenger transportation in Canada. This is visible in the choice of criteria that we have used. There are essentially five. First, the primary role of VIA is to serve the major intercity markets where there is a relatively high population density, by daylight services; over distances of 800 kilometres, which is 500 miles, or less. This is not original at all. This is what is happening everywhere else in the world. If VIA increases its ridership in recent years, it is mostly in these corridors-again banal to the utmost.
Secondly, we discontinue service or reduce frequency of service on routes where the ridership, the load factor, and the revenue-cost ratio are extremely low and have no justification. In some cases, you would be embarrassed if I were to indicate what some of the realities are.
Thirdly, there is one route that few people use. It costs the Canadian government $8.75 per passenger mile. There must be some limitation to the eccentricity of government spending!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: What route is that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Winnipeg-Armstrong.
Another point deals with the two Continentals. We have decided to maintain one, and not to eliminate the second one, contrary to what some press people have said, but to convert the second Continental in part into an intercity daylight system. We have decided to do this because of social, psychological, historical, economical and political factors. On balance, we think it is a good idea.
We eliminated one of the Continentals because it is the most costly part of VIA's operation. Half of the deficits of VIA are due to the transcontinental; about $160 million. I am not obsessed by money, because I am a Liberal!-I am not ashamed of that either.
The most important reason is that the northern transcontinental in Ontario and the west is used by people as an intercity system; it is not used as a transcontinental system. For the people who wish to use the transcontinental system, they will
October 20, 1981

have the southern one; and for the people who wish to travel city to city, which is the fact in most cases, we have decided to establish a number of intercity trains.

speechtext: Order, please. If the member wishes to ask a question, there has to be unanimous consent of the House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: These are again not original thoughts, Mr. Speaker. You will find them in the CTC final plan for western transcontinental passenger train service of October, 1977, If hon. members would care to read the latest report on trains in Canada, the Scrivener report in Ontario, they would find exactly what I am saying now. It says that northern Ontario people use these trains as intercity and recommends that the Governement of Canada change them from a transcontinental mission to an intercity mission.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Who's that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
That is the Scrivener report, in Ontario. I am sure you have read it.
The fourth principle or criteria has to do with the servicing of remote communities which have no adequate alternative mode of transportation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Like Armstrong.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
That covers Senneterre, Cochrane, Hearst, Thompson, Churchill and others. Armstrong is covered by Winnipeg-Capreol.
The fifth principle is simply that commuter-like lines can play an important role in transportation but they are the responsibility of the provincial and municipal governments.
My predecessor the hon. member for Vegreville agreed with that when he was minister of transport and said, "VIA is an intercity, not a commuter, railway". So I am in very good company with the former minister of transport, a Conservative, on this question.
The provinces have begun that process. Toronto and the Ontario government are in the GO system. Quebec is moving in a similar metropolitan system, taking into account commuter trains. I am quite sure that Mr. Snow and Mr. Clair in due course will take over responsibility for the trains that we have identified, that is Havelock, Stouffville, Barrie, Sherbrooke-Montreal. I am quite sure they will do it. It is much too early in the game to start complaining about the disappearance of these trains.
I wish I had more time to show that these changes had to come.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
No.
VIA Rail

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Yes, indeed, everywhere in the world. The world has gone through three revolutions, if not four. There has been the revolution of the private automobile, the revolution of the bus and the revolution of the airplane. Come and join the twentieth century! These changes have been taking place everywhere in the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Except France, Japan and Germany.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: I could give you chapter and verse which indicate that the same adjustments are being made everywhere in the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: There will be a revolution of the people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
It is not a revolution at all. There is a beautiful quote from the MacPherson report which reads as follows, although I think it is too rude:
The railways are accused of deserting communities by withdrawing passenger train service when a more objective view would be that the communities have deserted passenger train service.
It is not the passenger train service that has deserted people. People have deserted trains. Of people travelling in Canada intercity for more than 50 miles in 1977-78, only 1.2 or 1.3 took trains. I have all the figures here and they show that all the others used other modes of transportation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: According to Professor Fred Flintstone!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Even in Japan, the famous Bullet train which peaked at 157 million passengers in 1975 had declined to 124 million by 1979.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: But ours is going up.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
I should like to spend my last five minutes talking about why we did not go to the CTC. First of all, I do not have to take any advice about respect for the CTC; I am as respectful of the CTC as was my predecessor. Let me explain this to the House in four points. The first is this.
[ Translation]
It was within the law. The Leader of the Opposition realized that not long ago. At first he protested, saying that was not allowed under the act, pursuant to Section 64 of the National Transportation Act 1967. But why does the act permit the use of an order in council in that case? I shall tell you why. It is because there are circumstances where it is necessary to take a comprehensive approach instead of having recourse to the CTC, which relies on ad hoc procedure. There is no way we could establish a general plan by asking the CTC to make individual studies of each route. The only solution would be to issue the CTC, the Canadian Transport Commission, with guidelines that would include decisional criteria, which would amount to telling the CTC: Listen, first of all you will have a ceiling, like the Minister of Transport; your ceiling will be $500 million. Second, VIA Rail's essential role is interurban transportation; we think this is vital. Third, I think we need a transcontinental train. Fourth, make sure isolated communities
11984

VIA Rail
are protected. Fifth, listen, commuter trains are a municipal and provincial rather than a federal concern. Well, this is exactly what it says in the decision of July 27. In other words, to make the changes I would have had to tell the CTC: here are the criteria, here is a directive from the federal government, there is no other way we can carry out the changes we want. And obviously, if I had done that, as my friend Mr. Lang found out in 1976, everyone would have said: He is twisting the CTC's arm-
