subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Order, please. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. minister but his time is up. The hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) has the floor.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate and to say at the outset that we are in agreement with and will support the motion proposed on behalf of the official opposition by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). I shall move an amendment that I believe will also receive the support of hon. members on all sides of the House, or if not the support, at least the sympathy.
The motion proposed by the hon. member for Vegreville is very moderate. It only asks for a one-year delay, when I suspect that his view, the view of his colleagues and certainly my view and that of my colleagues, is that the order in council of the cabinet should be totally rescinded. To be reasonable, however, to be moderate, and in an effort to persuade the government to change its mind and at least restore some of the routes which are viable, we have opted for this mild, reasonable request.
John Kenneth Galbraith said that in the nineteenth century people distinguished between railway barons; there were those who robbed their customers and those who robbed both their customers and their shareholders. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) deserves the dubious distinction of robbing both VIA Rail customers and the taxpayers of Canada. The Jesse James and the "Lang gang" ride again!
Had this cabinet been in power in 1881, Mr. Speaker, it would have scrapped the idea of building a transcontinental railway. The simple minded idea of Reaganomics practised by this government is completely at odds with the geography, climate and the location of the people of Canada. In simple economic terms, if you follow the logic of the Minister of Transport to its conclusion, it would be much cheaper to close the St. Lawrence Seaway. There is a great deficit there. It would be much cheaper to shut down the railroads. There would be no need then for branch line subsidies, the At and East rates or bridge subsidies. If we follow the minister's logic, it would be cheaper to shut down the airlines. He moans and groans about the deficit incurred by VIA Rail. It has always been the case since this country was settled, and it has always been the case in every other country in the world, that not a single mode of transport ever paid its own way.
What does the minister want to do about the marine transport subsidies of $320 million last year? Under Section 64 of the National Transportation Act, he could shut down all shipping, if he goes to the exaggerated extreme that he has gone to in the order in council he passed regarding VIA Rail.
In 1979, air user charges were covered 38 per cent. What a cost to run our airports! There was a $476 million subsidy to airlines. The minister, if he wants to follow his transportation logic to its conclusion, should be shutting down airports and cancelling airline routes instead of acting like a fifteenth century Pope, dividing the world up between the Portuguese and the Spanish, by dividing up Canada among a bunch of airlines.
In addition to that $476 million deficit, the government wrote off $600 million worth of debt for Mirabel. One does not hear the minister moaning and groaning about that. On our roads and highways, our licence fees, fuel taxes, fines and revenues the municipalities, provinces and the federal government can recover only 55 per cent of the cost of operating, building and maintaining our highways. That amounts to a $3 billion a year subsidy for highway users.
Why is the minister picking on VIA Rail? I think it is because the Treasury Board and the cabinet told him to spend $100 million less and to pick out the easiest victim. He picked out VIA Rail and gave them two choices: it is either compulsory, or they have to! The president of VIA Rail was phoned up and given his orders to reduce services to save a supposed $100 million.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Talk about the number of people using these trains.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: The minister wants me to talk about the number of users. The number of people riding has been increasing at a record rate, far beyond what even CP and CN were able to do in their last three years. But it cannot increase any more with current policy. I am surprised that it has increased as much as it has while the minister, through government policy, has a mandate for VIA Rail to operate railway passenger trains on the basis that if one runs it old enough, late enough, slow enough and dirty enough so that no one will get on it, then one can cancel it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
That has been the practice. The minister and the government have victimized VIA Rail. They created the child and are now in the process of making an orphan out of it. VIA Rail got stuck for over $77 million worth of outmoded equipment which it should have gotten for $1.
The minister talks about $100 million in savings. There are built-in costs to that debt which VIA should never have had in the first place. The government started VIA Rail out in the same way it started the CNR in 1920 and 1921, with a debt which it can never live long enough to pay off. It is designed and set up to fail.
October 20, 1981

While every other industrialized nation in this world, even undeveloped countries, are making massive investments in new, modern, fast intercity and commuter passenger services, this country, which used to lead the world, is running 25 to 30 years behind. We should be making an investment, not in ten new LRC sets, but in thirty.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: The minister says he agrees. Well, how come the orders have not been placed? One needs three years of lead time just to get deliveries.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: We will, in the fall.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: The minister says he is going to save $100 million. He has already said that he is going to spend $30 million to help out those workers. He can make a decision which callously does away with 1,600 people, and he is going to spend $30 million to make it easy for them. That leaves $70 million in the first year.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Different accounts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Forty-eight per cent of the costs of operation are direct costs: wages, fuel-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: They are not.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Direct costs. There goes $48 million he will save. Where is the other $52 million? The other $52 million is going to get transferred to the remaining VIA Rail routes.
Past experience has shown that savings are not realized by abandonment. The minister has not taken account of the revenue lost from the routes to be abandoned.
By the way, I remind the minister, as he talks about the CTC and all the great respect he has for it, that the CTC held hearings on 15 of those 21 routes since 1976, and ordered that all 15 be retained. When the CTC spoke about the transcontinental routes, it said that they were at the irreducible minimum. So much for the minister's great respect for the Canadian Transport Commission.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
I have asked his department to give me a breakdown in savings, by each route. For some reason or another, I cannot get it. I wrote to the Minister of Transport on September 16. I first wrote to him on July 31, and he sent me a non-answer, signed by his parliamentary secretary. 1 wrote to him again on September 16. He still has not even acknowledged my letter-let alone answered it-concerning turning this subject over to the House of Commons committee on transport.
The $100 million that the minister throws around is apparently the $61 million in operating costs for the abandoned services, plus the estimated savings using LRC routes not being abandoned. That is stretching the point, to claim this to be a benefit of abandonment. Past experience shows that savings are not realized by abandonment. Forty-eight per cent
VIA Rail
is saved by direct charges: wages, fuel, maintenance. The balance of the overhead costs will be shifted to the remaining passenger services, so that more routes will show a loss, increasing their apparent losses, or costs will be transferred to freight services, which I do not see the CPR or the CNR readily doing.
The minister talks about Winnipeg-Armstrong. Is the minister unaware that the Winnipeg-Armstrong service is a mixed train? It pulls mostly freight cars and a couple of passenger cars, all of which is charged to passenger service. So much for his inexcusable excuse for a service from Winnipeg to Armstrong. He does not know anything about railroading. Anyone who would treat places such as Edmonton, Saskatoon, and our national capital, Ottawa, like backwoods villages is not deserving of the name "transportation minister".
Both the transcontinental routes, the Supercontinental and the Canadian, are used to capacity in the summer and in the peak periods of the wintertime, and the Atlantic Limited hauled 256,000 people last year; yet the minister wants to abandon them. That is not railroading; that is throwing up one's hands and giving up. One will not entice more people out of their automobiles and out of short-haul aircraft flights, which is the most inefficient way to move people, by having no trains. If one is not going to provide the equipment, the service and the schedules, why should people get on the trains which are left? I have a copy of the transcontinental passenger train schedule for 1892. Across Canada it made an average speed of 47 miles per hour. Does your Honour know what it is today? It is 39 miles per hour. So much for this modern revitalization by the minister of VIA Rail. On some of the routes which he now proposes he will have an average speed of 20, 22 or 29 miles per hour; and the minister wonders why no one will get on the train! What a back-asswards way to encourage people to take the train! What a way to set up a national rail passenger corporation! It is designed to lose.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: You should try riding the train.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
We are not talking out of some sentiment for the days of the steam engine and the wail of the locomotive whistle across the prairies. We are talking about the most sensible, economic transportation reasons for enlarging and revitalizing our national rail passenger transportation system. We should look at countries with geography and climate similar to ours, such as the Soviet Union and the Scandinavian countries, which have electrified over 100,000 kilometres of track. Trains are run at speeds of up to 100 miles per hour north of the Arctic circle. Australia has rebuilt its transcontinental railway system from Perth to Sydney. We should also look at what the Japanese, the French, the British and the West Germans are doing in rail transportation. They are making the investment, and the return on that investment is more than compensated for by the savings they make in other expenditures in other parts of their economies, whether in the construction of superhighways, fuel costs, environment or safety-you name it.

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
I do not understand the continual insistence on clinging to the 1890s concepts of rail transportation. The minister spoke about getting into the 1980s and 1990s, but he is still riding in the 1950s and 1960s when the CNR and CPR were trying to get out of the passenger business, and that is what he is trying to do as well.
There is no policy commitment by this government to make sure that VIA succeeds. This government wants to save $100 million by cutting back all these routes. But on the other hand, the government will turn around and spend, I predict, $100 million to establish a short takeoff and landing service for Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal, something we need like a hole in the head. Can you imagine anything so ridiculous, Mr. Speaker?
The Government of Canada has authorized VIA Rail to get ten LRC trains. They will cost over $100 million. They are to run along the Quebec-Windsor corridor. Now the government is going to establish a STOL service between Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto. But what is that for? The government will have two government agencies cutting each other's throats to get the same passengers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: But a different clientele.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
If the policy of the government is to get people out of automobiles and off short-haul scheduled airline routes by establishing LRC trains and competing STOL aircraft service in the Quebec-Windsor corridor, the minister has another think coming.
Instead, the minister is spending $100 million in each place for two government agencies to cut each other's throats. How ridiculous can you get? The minister does not know anything about transportation. He never has. He does not know one end
of a boxcar from another.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: He does not know one end of a horse from another.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
I want to move an amendment to the motion. If the minister will not leave this matter in the hands of the CTC, perhaps he will agree for the House of Commons Standing Committee on Transport to hold hearings. The government may want to make it a joint committee, I do not care. But by holding hearings, the people of Canada, officials of his department, the minister himself, representatives of VIA Rail and the railroads can appear. In this way the matter can be fully aired. We can give the committee until the end of June next year to complete its hearings.
There is another committee in this House besides the transport committee of which the minister is fully aware. This committee is questioning and casting some doubts on his and his cabinet's decision concerning the cutbacks. No hearings have been held concerning this matter. There have been no opportunities to rebut the reasons of the minister or of the executive, which has proceeded by fiat. The order has not been used to overrule a recent decision of the CTC, but there has
been a series of decisions extending back over a considerable period of time, decisions which have been acted upon and upon which the public had placed reliance. The public placed reliance on the decision of the Canadian Transport Commission on 15 of those 21 routes. I submit this is a breach of tradition in the country, even if it is a skilful use of the wording of a statutory provision, which it is probably fair to say is not designed for such a purpose.
If the governor in council can change the decisions of a commission, how far back can they range? They have ranged all the way back to 1976 CTC decisions concerning transcontinental passenger trains. Hearings were held before which members of this House from all sides appeared, along with members of the Senate. These hearings were held across the nation. The minister and the cabinet go back five years to rescind a decision of the Canadian Transport Commission. Yet the minister tells me about all the respect he has for the CTC.
This kind of massive abuse and misuse of Section 64 of the National Transportation Act means that the minister and the cabinet by order in council can cancel the rest of the VIA Rail passenger rail service. The government can abandon all branch lines. It can cancel all airline routes. It can wipe out the St. Lawrence Seaway. It can wipe out shipping. It can wipe out any damn thing the government wants to wipe out without any recourse to Parliament or any agency of government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: This is a shameful abuse of power.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
When the minister professes to me his respect for the CTC, respect for public input and respect for people who know something about running railroads, as far as I am concerned, he is a loser. I do not mind his losing so much, but I do mind when he causes the whole nation to lose in light of our energy crisis. Every other industrialized nation of the world, even underdeveloped countries, are buying our trains, our equipment, our technology and our expertise. But are we using it here? No, we are not.
It passes all understanding how the minister can get up and try to justify this kind of thing. We are not trying to justify the retention of all 21 routes, but I submit that at least half of them are viable. You cannot ignore places such as the national capital, the capital of Alberta, the second largest city in Saskatchewan, Jasper, Melville, Watrous, Raymore and Biggar. You cannot ignore the Jasper to Vancouver route. It is outrageous to ignore these places.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton):
That the motion be amended by deleting the third paragraph and substituting the following therefor:
"That this House refers the subject matter of order in council PC 1981-2171 to the Standing Committee on Transport to enable the committee to evaluate the economic, social, statistical and legal basis for the decision to ^diminish rail service, with authorization to hold public hearings and to travel from place to place in Canada, and instructs the committee to report its conclusions and recommendations to the House by June 30, 1982;"

I want to say one thing in quick passage, Mr. Speaker. Early on in the day the government House leader said that he would regard this motion as a vote of non-confidence. He knows that is false. That, I suggest, is a matter of fundamental importance to the functioning of this process.
Let me just say that we have often heard from the government, when we have raised questions, that if we really wanted to pursue those questions and really wanted to have them resolved, then we could have them raised on one of the allocated days, one of the days given to the opposition when we have the right to raise a question.
Now there is a new wrinkle being added by the government. It says we can raise those questions but we cannot have the government act upon them; we cannot have Parliament act upon them. It attempts to impose yet another muzzle on the rights of this Parliament to effect even our own agenda and our own freedom to act. It attempts in one more way to put one more shackle on the beleaguered backbench members of the Liberal party so they will not vote for their consciences and

their constituents against the arbitrary decisions of the government.

speechtext: All right, it was written in the 1950s and published in 1961; it is only 20 years out of date. subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
The Minister of Transport again trotted out figures which he knows are two to three years out of date- figures on passenger usage that he knows relate to the situation before the energy crisis forced more and more Canadians to use the trains. If he had held public hearings, as we did, if he had done what the CTC required him to do, he would have had the opportunity to hear first hand the evidence of people who have far more up to date statistics, statistics which take account of the impact upon the behaviour of the rail-using public of changes in the cost of energy, statistics which indicate that there is in fact more use being made of passenger rail service in this country than the government wants to admit.
The danger is not that the public is moving away from rail passenger service. The danger instead is that the government is taking away rail passenger service when there is no cause at all to do that on many of the lines that were doomed by his directive of July 27.
I should say that the other grave danger in substance is that we live in a time and in a country when there is an increasing fear that people, particularly in distant parts of the country, have interests and put forward positions that are ignored by the government at the centre. What better proof could they have if they live in western Canada and are served by the train through Jasper, or live in eastern Canada and are served by the Atlantic, or live in northern Quebec or northern Ontario, of the indifference of the central government to their interests than to have their rail service taken away absolutely arbitrarily, without any right to public hearing? This comes from a minister who served as a co-chairman on a commission on national unity. I cannot think of an act which could be better calculated to create disunity in this country than to take away the lifeblood of communities by an arbitrary act, without holding public hearings, thus breaking the CTC requirements and denying the public the right to be heard.
That is one of the issues here; that is the issue of substance. The other issue is the issue of process, the process of the denial of a public hearing. I heard the minister say that public hearings are difficult, and to have followed that route would have caused him all kinds of trouble. It would have required studies which would have taken some time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Four years.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Four years of studies to find the truth. I suggest it would have been better to have had four years of study that found the truth than to act in ignorance, in a way that disrupts the people and disrupts the services of this country, and does so for all time. In fact, he told us that Otto Lang had done it that
way. He said Otto Lang had followed the law. Otto Lang followed the CTC route and found he could not do what he wanted because too many people came up with other evidence. There is not much good that many of us on this side of the House would say about Otto Lang, but at least he had a better respect for democracy than the present Minister of Transport.
The other danger, of course, is that this proposal creates a precedent that is immensely dangerous for the country and for anyone anywhere in the country who relies upon transportation facilities under federal jurisdiction; that is to say, dangerous for anybody anywhere in Canada. The government has acted here in a way that wipes out public hearings. If it can do it with rail passenger service, it can certainly do it with any other kind of service.
The minister has used Section 64(1) of the National Transportation Act to take away 19 per cent of rail passenger service. What is going to be next? Will it be airports? He can with the stroke of a pen or the snap of his fingers do away with any airport under federal jurisdiction anywhere in this country. Will he do this next in respect of branch lines on the prairies? With the stroke of a pen he can wipe out branch lines on the prairies, no matter who has approved them or how valuable they are. Will it be done to the rest of the passenger service in the country, the other 81 per cent? It may be as doomed as the 19 per cent he has wiped out because he has the power. Will this involve ferry services on the coasts of Canada? The minister has the power to do this.
When the point was being made by my colleague, the hon. member for Vegreville, I heard the minister admit from his seat, and I think I quote him exactly, that hypothetically the law is there. Perhaps it is hypothetical today in the case of airports, but it was hypothetical in June in the case of 19 per cent of passenger rail service. Hypothesis becomes reality with this government, and once it gets away with using that kind of instrument to wipe out 19 per cent of passenger rail service, it will turn next to the target of airports it does not like, other passenger services it does not like, branch lines it does not like and ferries it does not like, all of this done without any public hearings, any respect for democracy or any concern for the current facts, rather than facts 20 years old, such as the MacPherson report.

What I wanted to advise the minister was that he might think it is legal but there are many people in this country who believe it is not. A legal action is being undertaken in the courts to test the legality of what he is doing. We know it is wrong. It may also turn out to be illegal. We will then have him on both counts, not only on the Constitution but also on VIA Rail. On the question of the Constitution we now have them on the count of it being wrong and divisive to the country if they try to proceed by legal trickery.
I wish to read for a moment from a report secured by the Toronto Star quoting a senior official of the Department of Transport. That official wrote:
Instead of using the section as its drafters intended-to vary the odd CTC order it did not agree with-the government is using it to restructure the whole VIA system. This is being done without CTC public hearings and without parliamentary scrutiny. Announcement of the changes was deliberately held up until members of Parliament had left for the summer recess.
That is not a member of the opposition speaking. That was an official of the Department of Transport speaking, indicating just how profoundly unpopular and wrong the minister's position is felt to be in his own department.
The government has bypassed the CTC in its hasty decision to dismember a vital national service. The CTC's role as protector of the public interest in transportation matters in Canada has been tarnished and diminished, if not actually destroyed. The minister will know that even in the United States, where attempts have been made to reduce the scope of Amtrak operations, those attempts have been extremely limited by the moderating influence of Congress which as a legislative body must approve budget cuts proposed by the administration.
VIA Rail
Since there are no safeguards in Canada, the role of the CTC is all the more vital. It has been cast aside callously by this government because they are afraid of the results.
It is interesting to ask why the Minister of Transport is reluctant to place the future of VIA Rail's transcontinental services in the hands of the CTC. The answer is clear. The CTC would have held hearings. It would have gone out and talked to people, as our task force has done. It would have gone out and listened to current data on current passenger usage instead of relying on three and four-year-old figures based on a period prior to the impact of higher energy costs upon passenger service in this country.
It is almost certain, Mr. Speaker, that if the CTC had been allowed to carry out its mandate that this Parliament gave it, it would have demonstrated that many of the figures used as a basis for decision are false figures.

The province of Quebec in particular will be severely affected by this unilateral and undemocratic decision. At least 225 railway employees stand to lose their jobs in the province of Quebec. Northern communities will become even more isolated. Communities located between St. Hyacinthe and Megantic will lose their rail passenger service. There will no longer be any service between Ste. Foy and Chambord. The train from Hull to Lachute will cease to exist. There will be no more "petit train du Nord". We have seen that the federal government, through this decision, has denied Canadians the right to a public hearing. This evening we shall see whether the voices of Quebecers are to be doubly stifled, not only through the absence of public hearings but especially if Liberal members from Quebec should refuse to defend the interests of Quebecers who are affected by this decision. We shall see whether the Liberal members from Quebec, in voting on this motion, will show that they are prepared to defend the interests of their constituents. If the motion is passed, the government will not fall, but the people of Quebec will see that the

federal Parliament of Canada is not powerless to defend their interests.
In communities which are to lose rail passenger services, many individuals will be severely affected. But that is not all. Behind this unilateral decision looms the ominous precedent the government has thus created. I shall be as brief as possible, because this is a very important matter. The Liberal members from Quebec have often mentioned the need for a strong federal presence in Quebec. They now have an opportunity to make their wish come true. The situation is clear. If the members from Quebec want the federal Parliament to be respected, today they will have an opportunity to earn that respect. They can show that the Parliament of Canada will defend the interests of Quebecers even if the government does not. Too often, when the legitimate interests of Quebecers are at stake, 74 Liberal members sit silently, afraid to speak out and afraid to act.
On the Constitution, the Quebec Liberal Party had the courage to defend the principle of federalism, but the federal Liberal members remained silent. When the Liberal government questioned the province's rights with respect to the sales tax, Liberal members failed to speak out. They remained silent about Mirabel, Nordair and the future of the footwear industry in Quebec. Will they also remain silent on VIA Rail, or will they support this motion and help the Government of Canada gain the respect of the people of Quebec?
That is a very important question, not just in Quebec but across the rest of the country, because this Parliament has the opportunity to speak up for and to defend Canadians whose interests have been severely injured. I ask any federalist in this House who wants to respect the rights of Canadians, who wants to be sure that decisions are based upon current information and who wants to ensure that we make decisions regarding rail passenger service now which serve the future instead of injuring the future, to vote in favour of this modest proposal to let the people be heard, to have a delay of a year of this unilateral abandonment of rail passenger service and to respect the right of Canadians to be consulted and to be heard on decisions which go to the heart of their personal and community existence.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great reluctance that I also rise this afternoon to address a few words to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). However, in answer to what the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has just said to the effect that the silence of Liberal members is such that nothing is being done in Quebec, I must tell him that he is very badly informed since I wrote the following letter to the minister on August 24, and I quote:
I find unacceptable the decision made, without consultation, by our department and VIA Rail to abandon rail service on the north shore of the Ottawa river on the Montreal-Lachute-Hull-Ottawa line. It seems to me that the Railway Act provides for public hearings when services are to be abandoned. Consequently, in a democratic system such as ours, I deplore the fact that this decision was made without consulting the population concerned.
October 20, 1981

On behalf of my fellow citizens, I therefore urge that this means of transport be maintained, or at least that public hearings be held so that we may know the pros and cons of this unfortunate decision.
And I, of course, signed this letter. I wanted to put it on record, Mr. Speaker, simply to show the Leader of the Opposition that he cannot take credit for all the work done in Quebec by Liberal members.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: This should be said!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
This is what I have just done, for the information of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle).
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, on September 25,1 sent a series of questions to the deputy minister, and my letter has not even been acknowledged. In this letter, I put the following questions to the deputy minister:
1.	Is there a cabinet decision concerning federal plans to revitalize and rearrange passenger rail services in Canada? Would it be possible to have a copy of this decision?
2.	If there is no cabinet decision, is there a document which confirms the will of the government and (or) the Department of Transport to outline this plan? Would it be possible to have a copy of it?
3.	As concerns the termination of passenger rail services on certain lines in the fall of 1981, do instructions outlining specific procedures for the abandonment of these lines exist within the government, the Department of Transport, the Transport Commission, VIA Rail Canada, Inc., the CN or the CP? If so, what are they and may I have copies?
4.	Do section 252 and subsequent ones in the Railway Act apply when the Minister of Transport decides to abandon certain lines used for passenger services? If not, why and under what authority are the minister and (or) the department exempted from these provisions?
5.	The line abandonment procedures will be initiated by whom, how, when and where?
6.	Can the Transport Commission hold public hearings for line abandonments and, if so, what procedure should be followed to get a public hearing?
7.	As concerns the Montreal-Lachute-Ottawa line, would you please tell me when the government intends to abandon this line? Which service and who is the official responsible for this matter in the Department of Transport?
8.	Under what authority can the government and (or) the Department of Transport proceed with line abandonments without consulting the population and without holding public hearings before the Transport Commission? Under what acts and sections of these acts do you have such authority?
9.	Are there mechanisms to appeal this type of decision and what are they?
10.	Are the plans outlined by the Minister of Transport in his press release subject to review? By whom and how?
In view of the urgency of the situation, I trust, sir, that you will be able to provide replies to these questions as soon as possible.
I am still waiting for a simple acknowledgement from a secretary in the deputy minister's office. And that is not all. Since we are talking about the VIA Rail file, I will not say anything to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) about Mirabel where I am also waiting for the transfer of flights from Dorval. I would refer the minister to a document published in a newspaper, not a large newspaper for sure, just a small weekly in my riding, La Petite Nation, but still the research work was done. According to a press release issued by the minister, two criteria must be met before abandoning a service. I will summarize what we were able to find about
VIA Rail
those two criteria. Judging from information release No. 13081 dated July 27, 1981 and issued by the minister's office, it would seem that the decision to do away with Montreal-Hull VIA Rail passenger services stems from two criteria: the cost-revenue ratio and the occupancy coefficient. The cost-revenue ratio on the Montreal-Hull line would be 0.15. By definition, that is the revenue quotient, or the ticket sales figures over the costs of annual services offered. Now then, with somewhat lower ratios for five trips, the minister does not urge complete abandonment but rather a reduction to three weekly trips. Here is the gist of his arguments: service is maintained because certain remote communities are involved. Therefore, the cost-revenue ratio is not a rigid index which automatically calls for abandonment. By virtue of the same principle, it then becomes possible to insist that the Montreal-Hull service not be suppressed. The localities of Petite-Nation and Lachute are far from the large urban centres of Montreal and Hull, which is the centre of attraction of our rural valley.
Let us refer now to the second coefficient, occupancy. On the Montreal-Hull line, that coefficient is estimated to be 20 per cent. We would have a 100 per cent coefficient if 1,000 passengers filled the 1,000 seats available. Here is how the minister justifies his recommendation that the service be dropped: abandonment due to poor performance, a good highway network, a daily bus service between Ottawa, Lachute and Montreal, and direct Montreal-Ottawa rail passenger service.
Well, Mr. Speaker, none of those reasons will stand close scrutiny. It is a matter of intervention. Consequently, there is no justification to discontinue the Montreal-Hull run in the eyes of the residents of Petite-Nation and Montebello where the economic summit was held and which was the focus of worldwide attention. Mr. Speaker, we have heard the promises of the PQ government; we were promised an expressway, but now it is still on the drawing board and may turn out to be nothing more than a skidoo trail. That is what they call good highway links. There is no public transit system in the Petite-Nation valley which is home to 17,000 permanent residents and swells to 30,000 people during summer. Unless you drive your own car, there is no way you can reach the tourist centres of Petite-Nation or Lac Simon, at Duhamel, whose economic fallout is essential for our region. We have a bus service for an aging population of which 9.4 per cent are over age 65, whereas elsewhere in Quebec the rate is hardly higher than 6 per cent, including 29 per cent higher than Quebec as a whole. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to address the government's policies of upgrading passenger rail services in Canada in order to meet the requirements of the next decade.
First, I would like to congratulate the hon. Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) for the courage he has shown in proposing a program to improve the efficiency of VIA Rail's services in Canada. Indeed, at the risk of being unpopular, the hon. minister is seeking a way to reduce substantially VIA Rail's deficit to help it upgrade its long-haul passenger services.
Over 30 years ago, the bishop of Gaspe, Mgr. Ross, said, and I quote:
-the lack of communications is the main reason why the Gaspe has lagged and is still lagging behind economically.
For the people of the Gaspe, the lack of communications and transportation remains a major concern.
Mr. Speaker, with the development of expressways in Canada in the last two decades, which was made possible through federal funding, and federal-provincial shared cost programs, Canada has become a country with one of the highest ratio of expressway kilometres per capita in the world.
VIA Rail
With the implementation of ARDA, the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Program, FRED, the Fund for Rural Economic Development, DREE and its agreements with the provinces, the Canadian government has helped the development of secondary road systems and service roads to natural resources sites, such as forests or mines. It is not surprising that with the development of such a good road system, some short-haul train services should lose some of their historic importance to the benefit of bus transportation. It is therefore normal under the circumstances that the Canadian government, through VIA Rail, should decide to reappropriate funds toward long-haul rail services.
Mr. Speaker, in the last few years, I have taken a very active part in the public hearings into rail transportation in the Gaspe area. The general criteria for improving the efficiency of rail services seem to be the following: relative cost-efficiency, distances between communities and important urban centres, elimination of duplication of subsidized services and the logical requirement of integrating short-haul urban transportation into the road transportation system. VIA Rail serves over 100,000 people in the Gaspe area from Matapedia to Grande-Vallee. For many, the train is the only available means of transportation. An economic study conducted by VIA Rail showed that in this area the train is the second most popular means of transportation for people.
Mr. Speaker, the Gaspe is one of those regions in Canada where an adequate rail service is warranted because of distances to large cities. Also, service would become more popular if VIA Rail could improve its quality by investing in the appropriate rolling stock. I would like, by way of example, to relate an event I experienced early in January 1981.
It took, at that time, over 58 hours to travel from Gaspe to Montreal, at an average speed of about 10 miles per hour. The Canadian Transport Commission report of inquiry into the reasons for this delay confirmed that it was a result of the poor condition of the rolling stock. A study conducted by the CTC on transportation in eastern Quebec and New Brunswick, following the delays that occurred during the Christmas holidays of 1980-81, found that in 43.5 per cent of cases, delays were due to the deterioration of the rolling stock. In 1979, after some hearings in the Gaspe, the CTC decided to reintroduce autorails from Matapedia to Gaspe, and the commissioners cited the same reasons.
I trust, Mr. Speaker, that the long-term savings achieved by the Department of Transport will enable it to improve transport infrastructures in the underprivileged areas in that regard, such as the Gaspe peninsula.
Generally, it can be said that the presence of an airport makes a wider area accessible to industrial and commercial activity through direct contacts with eventual clients; it also increases the volume of business. In addition, air travel encourages greater personnel efficiency by adding to the effective time on the job of management and technical staff.

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
Among other things, air transportation enhances marketing possibilities for perishable products, in that they can be shipped more quickly to consumer markets. The products of the sea and others would all benefit from being shipped by air rather than by ground transportation.
The activities of the fishing and tourist industries in the Lower St. Lawrence and the Gaspe peninsula are gradually being oriented toward more intensive and especially more rational development. Of the various facilities planned for those industries, the construction of industrial airports at Pabos and Sainte-Anne-des-Monts should be considered in the very near future. That is to say, Mr. Speaker, that the minister has become aware of the need for air transportation very recently as far as the Gaspe Peninsula is concerned.
The Ministry of Transport and that of Regional Economic Expansion must also plan on improving the infrastructure of port facilities in the Gaspe region and more particularly in Gaspe-Nord which, it will be remembered, lacks both railways and highways.
Mr. Speaker, I trust that the rationalization program of rail passenger services will allow VIA Rail to improve the quality of its services, thus enabling it to recapture its rightful share of the passenger transportation market in Canada.
The capital expenditure budget increase announced by the Minister of Transport on July 27, 1981 will further be used to modernize diesel cars and purchase new stock. The people in the Gaspe peninsula I represent in this House believe and hope that the cutback of less viable services across Canada will allow VIA Rail to improve services on other lines such as those in the peninsula and better compete with other modes. Moreover, the Ministry of Transport will now be in a position to invest more in marine infrastructures and the development of industrial and commercial airports in areas as remote as the peninsula. For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I will vote against the motion put forward by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), since the policies announced by this government have and will promote the development of other services in the peninsula.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in a sense I regret having a limit of ten minutes in which to make my remarks this evening in view of the fact that so many people across Canada will be adversely affected by the decisions taken by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) on July 27. These decisions will have a massive social impact on whole communities, businesses and individuals in Canada. In view of the fact that many members want to speak about these problems, I will restrict my comments to some of the quantitative implications of these decisions, and perhaps challenge the Minister of Transport on the question of energy, load factors, performance and cost.
I believe that the Minister of Transport has falsely, albeit innocently, informed Canadians on the question of energy and energy use as it pertains to our national rail transportation system. At the time of the press release at the end of July when the minister announced these cutbacks, he said, in part:
Railways are one of the least energy-efficient, energy economic methods, if not the least. Why? Simply because it is not energy economic to drag an empty car, and that is the situation now.
That statement is totally misleading. Before I came to this House of Commons I worked as a mechanical engineer and scientist. I can say with some authority that railway trains are the most energy efficient methods of all transportation modes. That fact can be substantiated quantitatively and firmly without any further controversy. In fact, a conventional diesel powered railway train operating with a high load factor will consume only about 700 energy units, referred to in the old jargon as British thermal units per seat mile, and an electric train will consume only about 150 energy units per seat mile, as compared with 2,000 to 7,500 energy units per seat mile for conventional automobiles, depending on the number of passengers, and 2,700 to 5,000 Btu's per seat mile for passenger aircraft. In other words, if we were to assume that all these various types of vehicles were filled virtually to capacity, the railway train would be at least four times as efficient and in many cases seven and ten times as energy efficient as our aircraft and passenger automobiles. In fact, the railway train is potentially more energy efficient than highway buses.
To illustrate: if one were to imagine a string of highway intercity buses with their rubber tires removed and attached together running on a railway track, those units would consume in total considerably less energy than if those buses were running individually on the highway, for two reasons. The first reason is that the drag that air produces would be much lower if you had a string of buses or a string of railway cars than if you had a number of individual units. The second is that the rolling friction on a relatively straight track is much lower for a rail borne transportation device than for a highway bus. In
October 20,1981

fact, the Minister of Transport is totally incorrect when he suggests that trains are one of the least energy efficient modes of transport. In terms of miles we can travel by train per gallon consumed, a modern efficient railway train will travel 400 to 500 passenger miles as compared to 20, 40 or 60 passenger miles for an automobile. An intercity bus, if it is operating at peak efficiency with full load, will obtain about 300 passenger miles per gallon. A Boeing 727 aircraft will obtain only about 35 pasenger miles per gallon. Therefore, one can go a great deal farther with a gallon of fuel by train than by any other mode of transport.
If we look at Transport Canada's own data as well as data from other sources, we will see that Canadian airlines are operating at an efficiency rate of something like 28 passenger miles per gallon. Compare that with the mileage you obtain with your automobile. Canadian automobiles obtain about 20 to 60 passenger-miles per gallon, but trains obtain 100 to 250 passenger miles per gallon. Even the old and antiquated trains operating today in Canada are able to achieve this.
Data from Transport Canada and from the bus industry indicates that buses operating on our highways are getting only 140 passenger miles per gallon. Therefore, we have the potential for saving vast amounts of energy if we encourage a gradual transition to increased rail use. This means that it is essential for people like the Minister of Transport to start talking trains and increased load factor, rather than dismantling the system, but he must encourage the ever-increasing efficiency of our rail transportation system in Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
As Canadians shift from highway and air travel back to passenger trains, the energy savings to Canada will be massive. Passenger rail services spend less than 5 per cent of their operating budgets on fuel compared to much higher fuel budgets for the airlines and the highway bus industry.
We might also consider that while trains used only about ten million gallons of fuel last year, buses used 20 million, domestic airlines over 700 million, and take note of this, Mr. Speaker, the conventional automobile consumed over 8,000 million gallons of fuel last year, or 8 billion gallons.
The more people are encouraged to change their modes of transport to the use of trains, the more we will decrease our dependence on that very precious and costly commodity, namely oil, particularly imported oil. Indeed, government policies which will reduce the availability of rail passenger services to Canadians will only serve to increase our per capita consumption of precious petroleum fuels, with a commensurate increase in the subsidy costs to all Canadian taxpayers.
In the last remaining minute or so that I have I would like to comment on a recent report released by Amtrak. It is dated May 20, 1981. This report reveals everything about Amtrak's operations to the American people, which is in total contradiction to the position which this minister has taken. Amtrak has released performance figures. Amtrak has told the American people just how well it has performed over the last two or three years. Amtrak has also instituted something called a route
VIA Rail
profitability system in which the cost effectiveness of all of the various routes served by Amtrak are monitored and regularly reported.
A most important conclusion in this report is that by converting to head end power in the United States, they have realized tremendous increases in efficiency as measured by the number of passenger miles per train mile. A most essential point is that passenger miles per train mile in the United States have been increasing remarkably on long distance trips. On the other hand, the passenger miles performed per train mile on the northeast corridor service, which is the New York-Washington-Boston sector, has actually been decreasing, and it is operating at a much lower rate of efficiency than the long distance services.
The point the Minister of Transport should be listening to, and I wish he would, is that long distance train service, rather than jerky, start-stop intercity service is, in the final analysis, much more efficient, and also more efficient than the modern type corridor system operated between Washington and New York through to Boston. Therefore, his suggestion that he is taking away from the regions their very essential rail service in order to benefit the corridor service between Windsor and Quebec City is, indeed, based on totally false economy. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I will attempt to keep my remarks within the ten minute limit so as many people as possible on both sides of this House can participate in the debate.
First I want to express my regret that the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), the former Minister of Transport, has seen fit to introduce this motion under Standing Order 58(9), which calls quite clearly for a vote of non-confidence in the government. The hon. member knows that, in spite of the rhetoric in the motion that says that, notwithstanding any Standing Order, practice or precedent, the House does not regard the passage of this motion as a vote of non-confidence, one cannot change the rules of the House by rhetoric. The rules are the rules. This is unfortunate because I suspect that had he chosen another route, he would have had some support from those of us on the government side because we are concerned about these cutbacks, as are members of the Conservative and New Democratic parties. The fact that these other routes, which are available according to the rules of the House, were not taken would indicate that the Tories, as usual, are playing politics with this issue, that they are not really interested, despite their words, in the effect cutbacks will have on jobs and on consumers.
Having said that, I should like to spend a few moments dealing with a particular cutback which affects the people of New Brunswick, and that is the cutback of the Moncton to Edmundston rail liner service. In a letter to the regional vice-president of the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway,

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
Transport and General Workers, the Minister of Transport said this:
The Moncton-Edmundston service is to be discontinued because of poor performance. However, alternate modes of transportation such as bus service through Fredericton and highway access to intermediate points on the train route are presently available.
I believe the minister has been very badly briefed on that subject. The facts would indicate otherwise. This rail liner service is an essential service to the northwest and central sections of New Brunswick. Without rail service, these portions of New Brunswick will be virtually segregated from the rest of the province and, consequently, the rest of Canada. With the cancellation of this train, citizens on the route will find it virtually impossible to go to Moncton and return on the same day to take advantage of the specialized medical treatment available in the city. It will also be very difficult for university students to get to the University of Moncton and back to their homes in northwestern New Brunswick.
At present, a resident of the Edmundston area can leave Edmundston at 7.30 in the morning by rail liner, arrive at
12.15	p.m. in Moncton, and have until 5.55 p.m. to conduct whatever business is necessary. He can then board the rail liner and return home by 10.40 p.m. at a return cost of $26 for an adult.
To travel the 586 road miles return by car would take at least 6 hours each way and would cost approximately $42. If you use normal business mileage rates of 25 cents per mile, the cost would be $146.50.
The only other alternative is to take the bus, leaving Edmundston at seven in the morning, have a two and a half hour wait in Fredericton, transfer buses again at Sussex and arrive in Moncton at four o'clock in the afternoon, leaving little or no time to seek medical or dental assistance. One would have to arrange accommodation for the night because the only time you can return by bus is the next afternoon at
2.15	p.m., arriving back in Edmundston later that night at a return cost of $62.50 per adult.
From an economic standpoint, the return cost by rail liner is $26, by car, using a conservative figure for the cost of gas, it is $42, and by bus the cost is $62.50, plus at least one night's accommodation.
I hope I have made it clear that the alternatives are simply unwieldy, expensive and not viable. I would plead with the minister, whom I know to be a compassionate and caring man, to reconsider his July 27 announcement.

speechtext:
I am also pleased, Mr. Speaker, to have the opportunity to speak on behalf of the New Democratic Party regarding the cutbacks in VIA Rail imposed by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). I believe the minister has been ill advised. He has bypassed the Canadian Transport Commission, a commission which is vital to the good understanding of railway transportation in Canada. The railway workers and the people of Canada generally have sent their representatives to hearings of the commission to present their cases. I think it is doing an injustice to the people of Canada to break and violate this vital and important link in our stream of communications. I say shame to the Minister of Transport!
After saying that, I want to say that the people of VIA Rail, not satisfied with taking over and promising improved transportation, have cut back from the 23 CPR Transcontinental cars which operated in the summer months to an average of 12 to 13 cars a day. As if that were not bad enough, the minister has now come forward and suggested eliminating completely the run from Edmonton to Vancouver. I want to comment briefly on that suggestion.
I have a letter that was sent to the Minister of Transport from the Municipality of Revelstoke signed by the mayor. I will not read the whole letter, but it says, in part:
-the City Council applied for 8 bedrooms to travel from Revelstoke to Vancouver on September 22nd, 1981 and return from Vancouver on September 25th, 1981. Although we applied a month in advance for reservations, we were informed that there was only one bedroom available on September 22nd, 1981 and none available on September 25th, 1981.
In addition, the minister is suggesting that we eliminate the northern portion of this very important route. We of the New Democratic Party toured part of central British Columbia and visited some of these areas. We received petition after petition, some from people in Prince George and Prince Rupert, many from chambers of commerce and municipalities, all urging us to insist that people from these areas be given the opportunity at least to be heard and to present their views.
When VIA Rail took over, there was a commitment to live up to past agreements with the railway workers. Let me refer very briefly to pensioners, the many workers on our railways who have worked long and tedious hours building up pensions which are, incidentally, very mediocre, and also building up pass rights on the transcontinental trains. When they apply to travel on these trains, they are told there are no vacancies. Shame on the Minister of Transport. Shame on the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), who was also a railway worker, sitting on that side of the House supporting that kind of drastic action which has been taken by the Minister of Transport.

October 20,1981

these mountainous regions, especially the poor and the elderly, have no opportunity to travel on these trains. Not only would they like to travel in them, they have no other alternative because there are no airports in this mountainous region.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Something should be done about it. I have asked the minister time after time, when will this section of highway be improved? CP Rail is not exactly innocent in this, either. It has sold 30-year-old equipment and, when it breaks down, not only do they charge for its repair but they charge for another diesel to help bring it up the hill. Then they have to take a yard engine, because it has a steam generator, and they bring it over and put it on a passenger train. They use any kind of patch-up work to get the train across Canada. When is the Ministry of Transport going to come forward with a transportation policy and a program to show the Canadian people we are entitled to an up-to-date railway system to give adequate service to the Canadian people?
We should not have to worry about whether the airlines will lose passengers. Many people cannot travel by air, they do not wish to travel by air.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government appears certain to carry out its directive to cancel 16 passenger rail lines nationally. These cancellations will severely hamper efficient passenger travel.
Two of the lines to be terminated operate in New Brunswick. One is the Atlantic Limited which carries somewhere in the vicinity of 240,000 passengers annually, despite the minister's protestations to the contrary. The second line is the Moncton to Edmunston line which was designed to operate as an intercity commuter service. It carries approximately 20,000 passengers annually. This line also serves such communities as Chipman and Minto. Both communities do not have any other mode of intercity linkage, contrary to the information the minister might try to pass on to this House in justification of his measures.
The Atlantic Limited is the most economical and direct link from Montreal to southern New Brunswick and the other maritime provinces. Saint John, New Brunswick is 473 miles from Montreal, and the trip takes 13 hours. If passengers are required to travel around the province and double back to southern New Brunswick on the Ocean Limited, as the minister proposes, the trip would be extended to 739 miles or 20 hours. The travel distance would be 76 per cent greater and the travel time 62 per cent longer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: What are the energy savings there?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
This unnecessarily long delay will promote energy consumption rather than energy conservation in an energy-importing region. It will promote isolation in an area badly neglected by the federal government.
At this point I would like to draw attention, as an example of the isolation and neglect of the federal government of the Atlantic region, particularly New Brunswick, to the absence from this debate of the minister responsible for New Brunswick. Where is the person who should be standing up and speaking on behalf of New Brunswick as New Brunswick's representative in the Cabinet? He has been stonily silent, icily silent.

speechtext: Who is that?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
He is the gentleman-I happen -to know because I occasionally see his face in the local papers-he is the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc). You would hardly know he is an individual who speaks for the rights of New Brunswickers in this House. Where is the other member from New Brunswick who should be in this House, the hon. member for Madawaska-Victoria (Mr. Corbin)? His region will be directly affected by the abolition of the line the hon. member for Moncton (Mr. McCauley) just talked about. That will directly affect the people in his constituency. He should be here as the voice of the people he represents just as we who are here are doing.
What hope do the people of New Brunswick or the people of Atlantic Canada have with this government? Obviously none.

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
This government refuses to listen. It refuses to care. During the last election campaign, why did the minister not come to Saint John, New Brunswick or Atlantic Canada and tell the people the government would take away their train if he was elected? Why did the government not tell the people of Atlantic Canada that if it came back to power it would force them out of their homes? Why did the Liberals not tell the people in Atlantic Canada that, if elected, they would reduce air services, increase the price of gasoline and home heating fuels? Why did they not do that?
The people are fed up. They are saying: What in God's name are we going to do? Let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, their plight is desperate.
The minister rests his decision on the argument that new equipment is necessary and can only be provided if these costly passenger rail services are eliminated. A better method of raising the moneys for this equipment would be to arrange a fair billing procedure between VIA Rail, Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. At their own discretion, CN and CP bill VIA for the use of its rail lines at an exorbitant profit. Sixty-three per cent of all VIA Rail expenses are paid for rail line usage alone. The actual unit cost of using these lines is unknown to VIA. However, it is known to the minister, the CTC, CN and CP. VIA president, Frank Roberts, maintained before the Standing Committee on Transport that if VIA is to operate efficiently, it must have some sort of fixed contract with CN and CP rather than be subject to the greed of these two megacorporations. In effect, Canada's passenger rail service is subsidizing freight transportation. Yes, Mr. Speaker, it is subsidizing freight transportation. Let the minister effectively deny that.
If CN and CP would deal fairly with VIA, the needed moneys could remain in VIA's coffers for the purchase of new equipment, without sacrificing 16 passenger rail lines. CN and CP are milking Canadians for a passenger rail service by the very mechanism they received in exchange for providing this service. CPR entered into an agreement with the federal government stating:
-in consideration of the completion and perpetual and efficient operation of the railway by the said Company, as stipulated in the said contract, the Government may grant to the Company a subsidy of $25 million in money and 25 million acres of land to be paid and conveyed to the Company... land for the right of way, stations and other purposes, and such other privileges as are provided for in the said contract.
These vast holdings have given the railways a moral and constitutional obligation to the citizens of this nation. The railroads should expect to bear a substantial proportion of the deficit. CN and CP should share the cost of this deficit.
When the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) was in Saint John earlier this month, he advised New Brunswickers that he was cancelling the Atlantic Limited for their own good. He told us we should be grateful that the federal government is taking the Atlantic Limited away from us. If he is sincere, if he believes we will be thankful that the transportation system hundreds of thousands of people in Atlantic Canada rely on
will be rendered useless and if he sincerely believes we will be happy, then he and his government are mad, or certainly deranged.
I recently presented a petition of some 11,400 signatures to the House of Commons. These signatures were collected in the Saint John area. The petition protests the cutbacks. Since that time, another 1,000 names have been added. I can tell the minister it is not a desired measure. Saint John is New Brunswick's largest city. Let the minister name one other province in mainland Canada which has its largest city not serviced by a major passenger rail service. There are none. Saint John has been cut off. Southern central New Brunswick has been cut off. Atlantic Canada has been cut off. The minister shows his indifference by getting up and walking out. From the point of view of this minister, the citizens of our region are nothing more than pimply pests on the posterior of time. The government will find out in due course just how pesky we can be.
I will leave a message for the minister, his government, the supporters of his government and those people who will stand this evening and vote against the motion put forward by the official opposition and the amendment put forward by the New Democratic Party. The message is from all people. Listen well, Mr. Minister, listen well to me; for if you don't, the last whistle that blows will surely blow for thee.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I support the minister's decision, and I am rising now to defend it. The minister has made a decision to invest in Canada's future. He has made a tough one because, as we have heard here tonight, there are many voices asking us to invest in small decisions which support inefficiencies and drain away the money and the capital we need for our rail system in the next ten to 15 years.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Tell that to the people who have to walk.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: I hear hon. members opposite from western Canada talking, and I ask them especially to remember that their region in this country is going to need $12 billion to $16 billion in new investment in railroads over the next decade. We want that money to be there, and we cannot afford to waste that money on empty trains which use up needed investment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: Just leave us alone. Let us make our own decisions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Last Friday the minister told us that every time a passenger gets on a train in this country, we pay $70 in subsidy. Three of us were in a taxicab after the minister made that comment. I asked the driver how far he would take the three of us for $210, and the driver told us he would give us a ride to Montreal, buy us tickets to the Expos game, wait around and bring us back to Ottawa afterwards. That is the kind of expense we are undertaking with these kinds of trains.
The minister has taken a fundamental decision which stresses three important points. He has said, first and foremost, that we must put a cap on the subsidies we give to the
October 20, 1981

passenger rail service in Canada. Five hundred million dollars is enough in subsidy. The minister has made the decision that there will be no blank cheque for the passenger rail service because we need the money for other rail services which are more productive. The minister has said that if VIA Rail needs more money, then VIA Rail will have to earn that money. Third, the minister has given VIA Rail the tools to go about earning that money. Despite the emotional claims we have heard tonight, he has not abandoned VIA Rail. He is supporting VIA Rail. He is giving that service the capital it needs to buy new rolling stock in order to attract new passengers and get more revenues so that the subsidies can go down.
We can hear the uproar, but we also know the facts. The uproar will die, and we hope the subsidy will die with it. The uproar we have heard here today is typical of the distortions which are happening in this debate. Let us make it clear that the very motion today, which our friends in the New Democratic Party call reasonable, says we are abandoning VIA Rail. We are not abandoning VIA Rail.
We have heard other distortions, such as that we are losing our passenger train service. We are not. We are reducing 19 per cent of the route miles that passenger service offers. That effects 1.2 million passenger trips every year, 600,000 of which are in my area, that is, Toronto. They are commuter trips. Those commuter services should be left alone by the federal government. We have no business offering them. There are three routes in the metro Toronto area on which currently we are doing a big favour to the Government of Ontario. We are paying $70 a head for 600,000 passengers in the metropolitan Toronto area every year. That is a cost which should quite rightly be transferred to the people of Ontario and not paid by the Government of Canada. We had acknowledgement of that fact from the government of Ontario. In its task force report, recommendation No. 4.7 on page six of the final report describes the geographic area covered by this commuter service. It is the exact same area that we are transferring to Mr. Snow and his colleagues in the government of Ontario.
I ask all members to pay close attention to that good Tory and good Liberal, a friend of mine, a man who knows his way around railroads, Paul Hellyer, who stated in a recent newspaper column:
At long last the government has decided to face the music. Inevitably, however, the reaction has been shrill and abusive-
It isn't surprising to hear the politicians yell blue murder because that's what the game of politics is like. But when the press climbs aboard, responsible politicians must wonder if there is any hope. Last week, for example, The Globe and Mail attacked government spending as the cause of inflation. Now it condemns the first serious effort the Liberals have made in a long time to cut expenditures. Cynicism is a two-way street.
