speechtext: Does the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) accept a question?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only have ten minutes, which does not permit time to accept questions. Perhaps if there is any time left at the end of my speech, I can accept the question.
All of the critics who have risen to attack this action have forgotten one simple fact. We have to come back constantly to that fact. VIA Rail cannot have, does not have, and does not want a blank cheque from the Canadian people. VIA Rail this year is costing the Canadian people $450 million in subsidies. We want that subsidy to be spent in the most effective and desirable way. We are prepared to spend that money in a fashion that will keep full trains running. We will also get new equipment, which is an investment in that railway's future. That is a fact that has been acknowledged and applauded by the president of the railroad, Frank Roberts, who says:
-now we've got a good basic system we can build on-
Roberts insists it will mean millions of dollars for badly needed new equipment. To be precise, it means $450 million over the next three years for new equipment. That equipment will not only be used, as has been said here, in the Quebec City to Windsor corridor, but will be used in Atlantic Canada and western Canada.
It will not simply be a shuffling of dollars from one railroad to another because we have written a costing order. It will be a genuine saving and a genuine investment. It will free up money that otherwise would not be available for the major investment and resource projects, in double-tracking, in the new Rogers Pass project and for the other projects that bring so much hope and are so necessary for the development of resources in western Canada and all across Canada.
No longer do we need to maintain worn out old patterns just because they are comfortable patterns. This country needs to look at its rail transport system. We need to invest in the effective, productive places.
We need to look at each of these subsidies and ask about their value. We should ask whether they are draining off resources that would otherwise be used for a stronger economic future. The minister has done that with VIA Rail. We have a lot more similar tough decisions to make along that line in the next ten years.
When we hear about this kind of local petty boosterism of encouraging people to go down to the railroad station and clap when the train comes in and then get in their car and drive home, to clap simply because the train was there, we must ask ourselves whether that is a productive way to build our future. Is that a genuine option? I do not think so.
The real option is one where we build a rail system that will endure into the next century because it is built to fill an economic need and to perform economically.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher), we hope, has gone a long way this evening toward realizing his ambition

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
to be chairman of the transport committee. The minister may look kindly upon his efforts tonight, although one can only look with horror upon the prospect of such a chairmanship, having listened to the hon. member tonight.
Many of the arguments for keeping the lines which have been abandoned by the government in this latest dictatorial move were made well and often this afternoon in terms of energy, jobs, national unity and tourism. I do not intend to try to go over them in the short ten minutes allotted to me. I want to emphasize a few of the points and, perhaps, bring in a few new ones.
Something we have not talked about with regard to the reduction of service in northern Ontario is the fact that many people have cottages between Winnipeg and Farlane in Ontario. As a result of this most recent announcement by the government, people will have no opportunity to go to their cottages on weekends from September through to June. That is a small problem on a national scale, but those people have made a big investment. They are among the people served by that line on which service has been reduced. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) as well.
The hon. member for Kootenay-East Revelstoke (Mr. Parker) mentioned the problem of passholders in general. The minister does not realize what he is doing to Canadian National passholders. The arrangement that VIA has with Canadian National Railways is that CN passholders can only travel on what were formerly or are at present CN lines. This proposal effectively disenfranchises almost all CN passholders. CN passholders in Winnipeg can only travel to Capreol. They cannot get to Toronto, Montreal or west. They can go north.
The pass privileges these people have received over the years as part of what was negotiated at the bargaining table has been taken away by the minister in one fell swoop. This falls particularly hard on pensioners who rely on their pass and tend to use it more than young people, particularly those who do not drive. Unless there is a change in the relationship between VIA and CN as far as pass privileges are concerned, there are many people, who now are unaware of it, who will be badly affected by this decision of the transport minister.
Part of the problem with VIA Rail is that they treat passholders as though they had some kind of disease instead of as people who have earned the right over a number of years by working for the railroad. The minister is here tonight. He has not looked up since I have started to speak.

He does not know what he is dealing with here. I come from a railway family. My grandmother lives in Biggar, Saskatchewan. She has a CN pass. My grandfather worked for the railroad as a car knocker in Biggar from 1912 to 1958. My grandmother will not be able to visit her children and grandchildren in Winnipeg as a result of the decision made by the transport minister to reduce service between Saskatoon and Winnipeg.
Those in Melville, Watrous, Rivers, a line I used to work as a pantry man, have been completely erased from the railway transportation system. I can tell the minister they will not forget it.
The last thing I want to say is that this is a test for the Liberal backbenchers to show whether they have any integrity. We want to know. We will be watching tonight to see where are the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Reid), the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae), the hon. member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), the hon. member for Timmins-Chapleau (Mr. Chenier), and the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mrs. Erola), members whose ridings are on the lines that are affected by these reductions. If they are here and have the nerve to vote against this particular motion, that is something that will be carried to each doorstep in their riding. I am sure each opposition party will promise them this.

People will be standing up one by one like seals voting against the interests of their own constituents. I can hardly wait to see this. In my heart of hearts, it will make me sick to watch this. We will probably see it happen. I have said enough, on this, Mr. Speaker. It is absolutely beyond the pale of this government to reverse the decision which it has made in such a dictatorial fashion. Yet it does not have the nerve to look people in the eye and try to justify this regrettable and stupid decision.

speechtext:
I hear the hon. member for La Prairie (Mr. Deniger) saying, "I spent many years under that direction." He would understand, therefore, the analogy that has been drawn.
This is a timely debate, Mr. Speaker, because the Parliament of Canada has been denied until today the ability to speak and discuss the abandonment of almost 20 per cent of the rail passenger service. Our party found it necessary to travel across the country this summer to let the public of Canada express its concerns and to state facts and information as to why the passenger service should be retained as it is at present. I believe there is reason for the people in the province
October 20, 1981

of Saskatchewan to present petitions and to make interventions and representations. For instance, the town of Unity, ably represented by Mrs. Leeson, said:
The federal government and VIA Rail's decision to discontinue through rail service is beginning to leave a bitter taste in our mouths. We feel annoyed, exasperated and, to say the least, very angry. Exasperated, because Mr. Pepin seems to be hiding from the general public in not allowing any public meetings to express our objections and concerns.
I should like to point out that the then Minister of Transport, during the time of the Western Economic Opportunities Conference, now Senator Marchand, said:
I am sure that it is also clear to the provinces that we will need to involve municipalities and that consultation at a local level is of essence.
This government denied the process: it did not allow the municipalities to make statements; it did not allow the public to become involved in its decision. The manner in which the present minister made the decision, without consultation, without public hearings, without parliamentary debate, has been criticized across the country.
I should like to refer to Mr. Homer Hallberg, local chairman of Lodge 1230 of the United Transportation Union at Biggar. He told the task force of the severe hardships and economic consequences if this cut of the northern transcontinental goes throught. He said:
It should be pointed out that the transcontinental service which VIA Rail is offering, will create hardship and inconvenience to anyone travelling from Saskatoon to Vancouver. Such people will have to change trains at Edmonton and go to Calgary to entrain for Vancouver, an extra 200 miles or more. And travelling east of Biggar, for example, passengers will have to stop overnight in Saskatoon or travel that far by some means other than train. There are many elderly people who, for medical reasons, cannot utilize other means of transportation, such as planes, and who do not have motor vehicles accessible to them. And what of young families who choose to travel "the way of the worry free"?
This was a representation made on behalf of the citizens of Biggar.
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Bockstael), is not in the House. There are about 1,600 railway workers who will be laid off because of the arbitrary decision. Approximately 225 workers will be laid off in the city of Winnipeg. If the hon. member wishes to protect the Minister of Transport rather than his own constituents, that is his choice. I believe he will pay dearly for that in the next general election because 225 jobs in the city of Winnipeg is an important matter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext: That is not right.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
The Minister of Transport is saying, "That is not right". So far he has not disputed the 1,600 jobs. He cannot dispute the 225 lay-offs. He will tell us, Mr. Speaker, $30 million is available for retraining. So far we do not know who will receive the money or how the money will be administered, and we do not know when these people will become eligible for it.
I should like to point out again what Mrs. Leeson said. She said:
What is the logic in running (the train) between Winnipeg and Calgary, when the ridership has been heavier over the CN route between Winnipeg and
VIA Rail
Edmonton and where it better serves Saskatchewan and Alberta, as CN runs through the more central part of the provinces?
I would like to give to the minister a little lesson on the geography of the province of Saskatchewan. The province runs about 750 miles in depth from north to south. The CP line he has protected runs within 100 miles of the United States border. I would like the minister to explain to the people who live 600 and 700 miles from that train service how they can take advantage of the transcontinental. I know he does not care. It would be nice for the people who live 600 and 700 miles away, to have some idea how they could avail themselves of this new equipment, this new capital that the member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) spoke so eloquently about.
The minister today, by his own admission, stated that capital will be needed and that we, in western Canada, we, in Atlantic Canada, and we, in Quebec and northern Ontario will benefit from the investment in capital. He said, "Two to three years for LRCs". But we will not do it in that time. It takes three years to have LRCs put on track. We have not placed the order. This is something we have to look at. The people of Atlantic Canada, the people of western Canada, the people in northern Ontario, the people in Quebec are paying for the additional service that the member for Mississauga North was so proud of. I can see why he is happy. He receives our tax dollars to guarantee a train service in Mississauga, and he receives our tax dollars to support the huge subsidy at Malton airport, which is right beside his constituency. He is happy. However, the majority of the people of Canada are being denied by the government something that is rightfully theirs and something they will long remember was denied them by the Minister of Transport.
I would like to point out to the minister the difference between his administration and past transport administrations. This is the first time in modern history, to my knowledge, and I stand to be corrected-the minister is a little older, maybe he can tell me-that Section 64 of the Railway Act has been used to cancel a train service, to cancel a passenger line, or to cancel a service. I look back to the Progressive Conservative government. During that administration, the then minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), used the act to put service in place. It was used to guarantee service that was scheduled to be moved out.
At one time, Section 64 was used by the hon. member for Vegreville to implement and maintain service for the line in northern Ontario. The service was increased, under the previous government, from three times to six times a week. The Atlantic was confirmed for retention following the CTC's recommendation under Section 64. For the information of the minister, the hon. member for Vegreville used the section to add to the permanent network additional branch lines, which are badly needed for the movement of grain in western Canada.
I would like the people in my constituency and the people throughout the east and west to know that if the minister removes passenger service by a sweep of the pen, he can also

October 20, 1981
VIA Rail
move their branch lines away from them and deny them access for their grain.
We have seen a commitment over the past number of years on behalf of several provincial governments and on behalf of municipalities to implement a transportation service. However, this minister is denying the majority of people in western Canada a transportation service. I find that totally incredible, Mr. Speaker. I do not understand a government that is raising the price of gasoline to well over $4 per gallon-which will cause great hardship and at the same time will remove the cheapest mode of transportation that is available to the people of Canada, namely, rail service.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few minutes to discuss the impact of the decision made by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), and to explain to my constituents why I am against this motion. First of all, Mr. Speaker, for the benefit of those who may be interested, in 1975 I was involved in submitting a petition to the Canadian Transport Commission, when the minister was proposing to abandon the line from Montreal to Mont-Laurier, more commonly called the "petit train du Nord". Because of the importance of this mode of transport for the people living in the lower and upper Laurentians, I felt that the Canadian Transport Commission should hear all arguments in favour of retaining and preserving the service. That is why my colleague from Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre) and I organized a series of representations to the Canadian Transport Commission to defend and support user interests. Unfortunately, and this was a great disappointment, Mr. Speaker, I received no letters or telephone calls supporting the action I took in 1975 in order to save this means of transportation. Some municipalities in my riding told me they did not write to say they were supporting my action for the simple reason that they did not feel the travelling public wished to go on using this kind of transportation.
In my presentations, Mr. Speaker, I said that if the travelling public had abandoned this means of transportation, it was for the simple reason that no attempt had ever been made to update the system. Equipment was obsolete. Anyone travelling in this part of the province of Quebec will notice that the trains are at least 25 years old and that service is poor, to say the least, while people who use public transportation expect to be able to travel and get to their destination at a given time and not to spend three hours on a trip that should normally take about an hour or an hour and a half.
Well, for all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, in 1975 I had to represent the interests of the travelling public, people who go to the lower Laurentians in the winter for downhill or crosscountry skiing and in the summer to the lakes and other scenic areas in my riding. However, in view of the lack of interest among the population and the travelling public in 1975, and despite efforts by groups such as the chamber of commerce in my riding and that of my colleague from Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle, it is clear that people are not really interested in using this means of transportation for travelling, and this is partly due to obsolete equipment, the system's unreliability and also the lack of regular services. For all these reasons, the people in the area and the travelling public from Montreal did not, in 1975, and still do not show very much interest in this means of transportation.
On the other hand, I would not like to see this system or mode of transportation phased out permanently. I would like to urge the minister-I see that he has left the House, temporarily I hope-I would like to ask him if in view of the test runs to be carried out in the Windsor-Toronto-Ottawa-Montreal-Quebec City corridor, it would not be worth while to equip the Montreal-Mont-Laurier line with modern equipment manufactured by the Bombardier company, for instance, which is making quite a name for itself internationally in this type of transportation equipment, which would provide the travelling public with a cheap, reliable and rapid transit system in any kind of weather. Perhaps the equipment could be tested in the same Windsor-Toronto-Montreal-Quebec City corridor, and then a case could be made for using the trains to facilitate access to the Laurentians and make it possible for people travelling to ski resorts and cottages in my riding to use this rapid transit system, which could easily compete with the conventional highway system.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I have decided to vote against the motion, because I believe that it does not represent the kind of action I would like to support since the inconvenience being caused to the public is being used to annoy and embarrass the government. I feel the present government is making a concerted effort to provide good administration by trying to cut unnecessary costs, and this includes the VIA Rail cutbacks, if we look at the number of people among the travelling public who use this type of transportation. So for all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I intend to vote against the motion. However, I would ask the minister to ensure that results of the test runs to be made in the Windsor-Montreal-Quebec City corridor will be used to provide this area with a satisfactory, modern and rapid transit sytem in the years to come.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on this motion. I know of no other issue that has so inflamed the hearts of Canadians, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, than the announcement in July by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that the government will cancel 13 railway passenger routes and reduce six others, thus cutting from four to two our transcontinental runs, effective next month.
October 20, 1981

This 19 per cent cut in rail passenger service across Canada has been hailed by the minister as a vital step in the restructuring and reshaping of VIA Rail. I can tell the minister, quite frankly, that it is looked upon as a major disaster and a slap in the face not only for Nova Scotians but for all citizens of Atlantic Canada. This decision is illogical, it is discriminatory and it is counterproductive. It is the first time in the history of this nation that a federal government has decided arbitrarily to eliminate railway passenger service on such a massive scale without the benefit of public hearings, the opportunity for parliamentary debate or examination by the Canadian Transport Commission, a body set up to protect Canadians from this type of dictatorial action.
The government's attitude toward the people it was elected to serve is quite obvious as set out in a letter signed by the Minister of Transport on August 31 and directed to the executive secretary of the Canadian Railway Labour Association. In view of the limited time available to me, I shall not quote all the letter but on page 2, in paragraph 2, the minister stated:
The recent cabinet decision was one of policy and within that policy little discretion would have been left for the CTC in its application-as funding limits and train role priorities were declared.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, this is not just a decision by the federal Minister of Transport; this is a decision that has the approval of the entire cabinet. The government is saying, in effect, "We will take no notice whatsoever of the regulatory body called the Canadian Transport Commission, except when it suits our purpose. Again, we will take no notice of Parliament and on this issue we will not even bother to consult with members of Parliament, the people's elected representatives, because such consultation at this time would not suit our purpose. We will, rather, bulldoze this through cabinet against all opposition and in defiance of our constitutional rights and obligations which include a commitment to provide this nation with adequate transportation facilities." That is what the government is saying. By a simple cabinet directive, the government is implementing a cutback which would affect 1,200,000 passengers and some 1,600 railway employees.
A century ago our government leaders, some of whom were Liberals, developed and encouraged our present railway system in order to enable Canada to become the country that it is today. At that time, there was no alternative but to knit together such a far-flung region into one country, and it is no less true for us today. Fifteen railway lines are to be discontinued, leaving many communities without rail or air transportation. This cannot help but encourage a feeling of isolation and the growth of regionalism which many Canadians are now supporting. If Canadians have ever before doubted that this Liberal government was out of touch with the country it governs and its people and unconcerned about their problems, they now have ample evidence of it with this cutback in rail service.
I cannot help but wonder as a Nova Scotian how much more Canadians will have to endure before they stand up and
VIA Rail
demand accountability from those they put in office to look after their affairs. Certainly, they cannot accept the present state of affairs which has brought about low productivity, unimaginable delays, and wrangling over vitally important energy development projects, uncontrolled inflation, crippling interest rates, a monstrous public debt, a substantially discounted dollar, and constant confrontation between business and government.
Is it any wonder that foreigners who see this country as being rich beyond description in resources question our inability to achieve economic wellbeing because we accept and condone stupid, non-starter policies such as this cutback in rail service? That is the kindest description I can give it. This change must be made, says the hon. minister, in order to save the taxpayers money. However, in what has been termed by some Canadians as the next golden age of trains, this may well be a move which is penny-wise and pound-foolish.
In the maritimes, and in my area in particular, the announcement of the cancellation of the passenger train service between Moncton and Edmundston, New Brunswick, and the major train, "the Atlantic", which links Halifax, Moncton, Saint John and Montreal, has raised fear that the railways may also abandon more freight lines. More important, they may seek to abandon, by a stroke of the pen, some of our ferry services which are so vital to us in Nova Scotia and in Atlantic Canada. This would deprive Canada, and Atlantic Canadians in particular, of an essential tool in getting our goods to markets in central Canada and the United States.
I say to Your Honour that the question must be asked: are the savings of VIA not offset by increased costs to other branches of government required to deal with increased unemployment? The answer, of course, is yes. There was no indication in the government's announcement that this side of the problem was even considered in any manner whatsoever.
In my constituency, the government's attitude toward the provision of adequate passenger and freight service through the railroad has been of some major concern for some time. It started with a press notice on November 5, 1980, which closed out 11 express agencies, seven of which were on the south shore. There were strong objections raised to this move at that time, all to no avail. Later, there were strong objections raised to the government's plans to abandon freight service between Liverpool in Queen's County and Yarmouth, Nova Scotia. The minister also paid no attention to any of these pleas, all of which I, as the member of Parliament for the area, supported in committee and with speeches in the House.
I ask Your Honour, how much has the minister saved by that action? According to the records, in the last five years, the line between Liverpool and Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, lost only $3.5 million; and although this government could not find the money to provide a service for five years on the south shore of Nova Scotia, it could, at the same time, write off $600 million of a debt owed by Mirabel, the biggest white elephant in this country's history.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 58-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-VIA RAIL-CUTBACKS IN PASSENGER SERVICE
speechtext:
According to the government's own figures, 625 businesses a month went bankrupt in the first eight months of this year, at a cost of $633.5 million. In the same period last year, 540 firms a month went bottoms-up, at a loss of $475.6 million. How many businesses must go to the wall, along with the shattered dreams of their owners and lost productivity to this nation, before this government which sits on Your Honour's right wakes up and realizes that its policies are not working and that its programs are leading this nation in the wrong direction, as is the present railroad policy?
I say that if this government wants to save money, I will not only be critical but I will give a concrete suggestion which will save many millions of dollars. This can be done by simply discontinuing the government's policy of providing free icebreaking services to users of the St. Lawrence River. In my view, these services should not be free to commercial shippers using Montreal, any more than railway services or ocean terminal services are free to international shipping lines which are using Halifax, Nova Scotia. I also think the time has come for this federal government to examine the state of Canada's containership industry, especially with regard to its operations on the east coast. I urge this federal government to abide by the terms of the National Transportation Act and to equalize the situation between eastern Canadian ports to that we can compete on a fair and equal basis.
We do not seek charity in Atlantic Canada; but I tell the government, through Your Honour, that we do seek justice.
Finally, I must put the following questions to this government: do we want trains made in Canada, using made in Canada electricity, running on made in Canada rails, providing Canadians with comfortable, low-cost, convenient service; or do we want jets made in the United States, using extravagant quantities of imported oil and heavily subsidized airport facilities? Trains are the most energy efficient means of land transport known to man. We as Canadians are sadly in need of new routes and upgraded tracks in order to become competitive and more productive. I suggest that we get the unemployed off the unemployment roles and put them to work building railroads, for so doing, we will really be rebuilding Canada and providing a much needed service to all Canadians.

speechtext:
In those days I had the opportunity to travel everywhere in Canada and to realize just how important the Canadian railways are to the people. I saw with my own eyes the importance of Canadian railways in the villages of Saskatchewan, I saw it with my own eyes as well in the maritime provinces because indeed, Mr. Speaker, the railways played a big part in the building of this country. As a politician it is not easy nowadays to hold the transport portfolio, and I must admit that I have every respect for any transport minister when he has to act as such during a period of budgetary restraints because, as it happens, it is precisely during periods of budgetary restraints that the most difficult decisions must be taken, that a choice must be made. And that choice, Mr. Speaker, was simple. It was obvious and it required a decision which could not be put off. The choice was as follows: are we going to maintain the existing VIA Rail routes, with equipment which all members agree is outmoded, through a company whose deficits are altogether unreasonable, or are we going to strengthen the tree by pruning a few branches so as to make sure it will regain its energy and vigour?
Mr. Speaker, I must admit that, faced with a decision which, politically and in the short term, will have serious consequences, but which will have beneficial economic consequences in the long term, as a government member, I must support wholeheartedly the views of the Minister of Transport because, in the short term, Mr. Speaker, no one wants to lose his train service and, of course, the members of the opposition are doing what I would perhaps do myself if a train service were to disappear in my constituency, as there is indeed a commuter service which will be abandoned. If a passenger service in my constituency were to be abandoned for good, I would do what they are doing and I would criticize the decision of the Minister of Transport because this is what they must do in the opposition in the short term.
However, this is not what you should do, Mr. Speaker, when you form the government and have long-term economic responsibilities in a period of budget restraints as is the case now. New equipment is the new blood which is going to rejuvenate the Canadian railway network for a better service. What will a better service give us? More users and more
October 20, 1981

revenue! Therefore, we have no choice but to accept in the short term that some routes be abandoned. But what does this mean exactly? People are under the impression that those will be gone forever. But if we believe in the railway passenger service and in people in authority like Frank Roberts, whose ability and integrity cannot be questioned by anyone in this House, we must realize that this decision, which is necessary, is in the best interests of all those who want a railway passenger service in this country. This seems obvious to me. And what shall we do with the money that this will save, Mr. Speaker? It will be redistributed in all the areas of the country affected by these abandonments. It will be used to reduce the deficit, to acquire better equipment and to provide a better railway service. Still, this decision is criticized. I can understand this. I accept the reasons for this in the short term.
I was listening to the former Minister of Transport, the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), when he said at the very beginning of his speech this afternoon that he wanted an adequate railway service for Canada. I underline the word "adequate", Mr. Speaker, because what I want myself is not an adequate railway service, but an excellent railway passenger service. If we want an adequate service, we only have to keep what we have now, that is old equipment, more or less reliable routes and a mediocre schedule, but if we want an excellent service, if we really want to provide the service that the population should expect, we need new equipment, and this takes money. This money must come from savings and these savings will come from cutting back on the lines which are operated at a deficit.
Let no one suggest that this decision is illegal because I know quite well that all the ministers of Transport in the past, including the hon. member for Vegreville, have used Section 64(1) to make sure that their actions were legal. There is therefore nothing illegal in this decision, Mr. Speaker; it is perfectly legal. I am certain that if the Progressive Conservatives make good on their threat, that is, to ask for an injunction against the Canadian government, their request would be denied. The saving is purely artificial because what the railroads do not get out of VIA, they will collect in freight rates. Do not forget that.
The other thing that you should remember is that VIA was saddled by this government when it was initially established
with a cost structure differing from that of the railroads, which made it impossible for VIA to become viable. VIA was never intended to be viable. It was never intended to operate as do the systems in Japan, as does Amtrack or as do the systems in Britain or France. It was intended to fail and it was doomed to obvious failure when it was saddled with paying 64 per cent of all its expenditures to CN and CP. Every nickel that is taken out of their coffers is taken out of taxpayers' pockets through increments in freight rates. That is a false saving.
This says nothing about the fact that perhaps $40 million will be lost in Japanese tourism on the west coast, nothing about strangulation of tour plans by VIA and those in the Annapolis Valley, and nothing of tourists who came in from the Atlantic and go to Prince Edward Island and on to Newfoundland. The government is saving money on the backs of every Canadian who is in the tourist business, every one of them. The government is saving money at the expense of senior citizens who prefer to ride on the trains. The government is saving money at the expense of students who travel-and we talked with them from coast to coast in Canada-by the cheapest means of transportation they can find in Canada; the government is saving money on their backs including the backs of people in Moncton. The government is saving money at the cost of inconvenience of the disabled, who made several presentations to point out that for the sake of economy, convenience and comfort, not otherwise available, they travel VIA Rail in practically every instance. The government is saving money at the expense of those who for health reasons cannot fly, and it is saving money at the expense of those who cannot drive. The government is saving money at the expense of the servicemen of this country who are posted far from home with inadequate incomes to travel by any except the cheapest means at their disposal, and saving money at the expense of the small businessman who cannot afford to travel by air, and there is a multitude of them definitely using VIA Rail. Those are the people on whose backs the government is saving money. It will have to transfer this to freight rates when the railroads have to collect the difference. The government is saving money at the expense of several thousand people. Some 1,600 will be dismissed, and what is the multiplier factor? If it is 7, we are looking at something like 10,000 jobs which will disappear directly or indirectly as a result of cutbacks in rail transportation. That is how the minister is saving money. Mr. Speaker, I thank you for this opportunity to speak about the future of rail transportation in Canada, and especially the service to northern Ontario. Throughout our history there has been an assumption that transportation, especially cheap transportation, was too important to allow economic considerations to interfere with service. National unity, economic development and frontier settlement were far too critical to apply a real dollar value to them. But today, anyone who speaks about passenger train transportation in Canada has to refer to the
October 20, 1981

economic realities of cost ratios per passenger; that is, the cost to the taxpayer for every passenger who boards a train.
The fact is that every time a passenger steps on a train in Canada, the taxpayers pick up two thirds of the fare. Even with the $500 million in subsidies VIA Rail receives, the chances of a full recovery of our passenger systems are very slim. The Canadian people pay $410 million to VIA just to cover their operating losses, even if they do not travel by train. Passenger service on the scale we now have is simply too expensive.
We had hoped, with the introduction of the VIA system in 1977, that profits could begin to lower the deficit of our passenger system. This was the motive of the transportation acts introduced in 1977. At that time the Crown corporations involved in passenger transport were directed to strive toward making a profit.

Mr. Speaker, I will set my pace to a speed at which hon. members can understand me.
Opponents of rationalization say that trains have to be considered a public service and they have to operate in the public interest. But the public interest also includes fiscal responsibility, reducing the federal deficit and, hopefully, inflation.
A good example of the cost ratio for a route in northern Ontario is the route from Senneterre, Quebec, to Cochrane. For every passenger on this route, the taxpayer has to pay 77 cents for every dollar of cost. With only a 25 per cent occupancy rate, this train is not efficient enough to continue service once a day. This service has thus been cut to three times a week. This major link between Cochrane and Montreal is not fully utilized, and economic considerations have to outweigh the desirability of continuing this route on a once a day basis.
The line from Capreol to Homepayne is very similar, with a .05 per cent cost ratio and an 11 per cent load factor. There are other services that are even less efficient. I refer to the route between Sudbury and White River.
However, pure economic rationalizations do not take into consideration the very special needs of northern Ontario. There are many communities in the north which are rail dependent. Some of these have other links to the rest of the
VIA Rail
province only on a seasonal basis. If pure economic considerations are applied to these rail links, the fragile social and economic environment of these isolated communities could be disrupted forever. As a member of Parliament from northern Ontario, I am attempting to convince the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that these rail lines have to be protected.
I am not, however, advocating that the minister return these lines to the service levels they had before the announced cuts. What I am saying is that the Canadian Transport Commission and the provincial and federal governments have to explore the possibly alternatives to the types of service provided before.
You may note that the Minister of Transport this afternoon talked about the Scrivener report under the Ontario government. I have here a motion from the Northeastern Ontario Municipal Association, an area in which the Conservatives failed to hold a hearing. This is the only place in which they turned down the opportunity to hold a hearing. In any event, the association moved a motion which I should like to quote. It states:
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That the Government of Canada be requested to initiate a study jointly with the Government of Ontario, using the Scrivener Task Force brief as a guide, and with input from the public, on the present and future needs of rail passenger service in Northern Ontario.
What we do not need is more costly public hearings. Hearings on northern transportation systems have resulted in the same conclusions since the first royal commission on transportation in the 1920s. There have been, as you will recall, hearings within the last four years as well, and the answers and conclusions of those commissions were obvious to all of us. The conclusions were that these services are considered to be vital communications links which have to be maintained in the public interest.
We all know that the service is not economically efficient yet. We also know that it is vital to many of our neighbouring communities. No one could possibly disagree that we have to fight to maintain local service.
